“Like ‘Don Barry,’ the film is about aging, but seen from childhood instead of old age,” Smart said. His goal is to show the film this winter at festival premieres that have already honored him.

Smart is not only a filmmaker and radio producer, but also the author of the memoir “With Different Eyes: A Covid Waltz in Words and Images.” He has also written a novel: “Overlook: A Rock and Roll Fable.”

He believes that nurturing creativity is much easier in a country like Mexico, where capitalism is less “predatory” than in the U.S., and where not all values are economic.

“One of the first things I saw and appreciated here was the way all elements of life are allowed to coexist … the ugly and beautiful, life and death, rich and poor, dirty and clean. Some call it surrealism, others a wider appreciation of life,” he wrote in an email.

Whichever it is, the rich, heady atmosphere in Mexico provides the oxygen that enables Smart to keep creating.

Louisa Rogers and her husband Barry Evans divide their lives between Guanajuato and Eureka, on California’s North Coast. Louisa writes articles and essays about expat life, Mexico, travel, physical and psychological health, retirement and spirituality. Her recent articles are available on her website, authory.com/LouisaRogers.

World.title: Spanish police confiscate dozens of critically endangered Mexican axolotls
World.content:
Spain’s National Police have recovered 29 axolotls, a critically endangered amphibian endemic to Mexico that survives in the wild only in the canal system of Xochimilco in Mexico City.

Spanish authorities confiscated the specimens in the city of Granada and are investigating a Mexican national for his alleged participation in illegally trading the axolotls.

Although the International Union for Conservation of Nature classifies the axolotl as a critically endangered species — the category immediately preceding extinction in the wild — its international trade is legal, though strictly regulated.

The species is included in Appendix II of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora. As such, international trade must be controlled and supported by the necessary documentation to prove the legal origin and traceability of the specimens.

Spanish authorities say the suspect did not have the proper documentation. Therefore, they seized the axolotls and are pursuing charges of unauthorized possession and sale of specimens of a protected species.

Meanwhile, the axolotls are under the supervision of specialized veterinary personnel at the Zoobotanical Biodiversity Conservation Center of Jerez de la Frontera, in Cadiz.

The natural population of axolotls in Mexico has suffered a marked decline as a result of habitat destruction and degradation, water pollution, urban sprawl and the introduction of invasive species into the Xochimilco canal system.

This precarious situation contrasts sharply with their growing popularity as pets, making it especially important to control the origin of these carnivorous amphibians and prevent demand from fueling their illegal trade.

Even so, Mexican media have reported that axolotls are illegally sold (for around 500 pesos, or US $30) at the Mixhuca Market in the Venustiano Carranza borough of Mexico City.

In addition to Europe, the illegal trade reaches as far as South America, where Chilean officials confiscated 65 axolotls in April. Chilean officials have estimated that nine in 10 axolotls die of asphyxiation, dehydration or exposure to extreme temperatures during the transition.

Although appreciated as exotic pets, a lack of adequate information and unsuitable captive conditions endanger the lives of these amphibians. Placing an axolotl in a fish tank with clean water overlooks the reality that they are an extremely delicate species with very specific needs.

With reports from LopezDoriga.com, El Heraldo de México and N+

World.title: Cox to build US $310M desalination plant in Baja California
World.content:
Spanish company Grupo Cox will build a long-awaited desalination plant in Rosarito, a coastal city in the drought-prone state of Baja California.

The National Water Commission (Conagua) last week awarded a 5.29 billion-peso (about US $310 million) contract to Cox to build both a desalination plant and its pumping station in Rosarito, a town located south of Tijuana on the Pacific coast. The company submitted a bid for the project as the leader of a consortium that includes Mexican company Gami Ingenieria e Instalaciones.

Cox, which has a Mexican subsidiary called Cox de México, acknowledged Conagua’s decision in a statement released on Monday.

“Cox, an international group specializing in critical water and energy infrastructure, has been awarded, through a public tender process, the construction of the Rosarito desalination plant in Baja California, Mexico,” the company said.

“The project, promoted by the National Water Commission (Conagua), represents an investment of US $304 million and will help strengthen water security in the region, benefiting one million people during its first phase,” said Cox, which evidently calculated the cost in dollars using an outdated USD:MXN exchange rate.

The company said that the plant — which has been in the works for years — is “one of the priority initiatives under Mexico’s National Water Plan and will address the water supply needs of Playas de Rosarito and the south-western area of Tijuana.”

Enrique Riquelme, Cox’s executive chairman, said that the desalination plant project “reaffirms our commitment to Mexico following the acquisition of Iberdrola Mexico.”

“Through this award, we are bringing our expertise in the water sector to a country where we continue to support the development of infrastructure that contributes to people’s well-being and to the country’s sustainable growth,” he said.

“We are proud to collaborate with federal and state authorities on an initiative aligned with the objectives of the National Water Plan and one that will help strengthen the region’s resilience to the challenges associated with climate change,” Riquelme said.

Cox: Desal plant will produce 190 million liters of drinking water per day in first phase

Cox said that the first phase of the project includes the construction of a desalination plant with the capacity to treat 2,200 liters of seawater per second, “enabling the incorporation of approximately 190 million liters of drinking water per day into the regional water supply system.”

The company said that construction of the plant is expected to be completed in three years.

“Cox will be responsible for the engineering, procurement of specialized equipment and construction of the infrastructure, which will provide a complementary and independent water source from the Colorado River, strengthening water resource availability in Baja California,” Cox said.

“The desalination plant will have a final production capacity of 4,400 liters per second, equivalent to more than 380,000 m³ [380 million liters] of drinking water per day, making it the largest facility of its kind in Latin America,” the company said.

Cox said that the plant will use “reverse osmosis technology, an advanced treatment system that employs semi-permeable membranes to remove salts, minerals and impurities from seawater and convert it into drinking water.”

This technology is recognized for its high operational efficiency, the quality of the water produced and its lower energy intensity compared with other desalination solutions,” the company said.

Cox noted that it operates desalination plants across 16 countries with a combined desalinated water production capacity exceeding 4.4 billion liters per day.

The public tender process

Cox’s 5.29-billion-peso bid for the desalination plant project was the lowest among three participants in Conagua’s public tender process.

The score for its proposal — 94 out of 100 — was higher than those given to one consortium led by Acciona Agua México and another led by Tecno Arrendamientos y Construcciones.

The federal and Baja California governments will jointly fund the desalination plant.

Two previous tender processes for the desalination plant failed to find a company that was able to meet the technical and economic requirements of the project. Consolidated Water was previously contracted to build the plant, but the Baja California government canceled the company’s contract in 2019 and a lengthy legal dispute ensued.

With reports from Expansión, El Sol de México, EFE and BNamericas

World.title: Bilateral security cooperation nets more fugitives, including several priority US targets
World.content:
U.S.-Mexico cooperation on security matters has netted another criminal destined for extradition, sending a clear message: “Whatever the crime, criminals have nowhere to hide.”

Jalisco police officers captured a man identified as Antoni Covarrubias in Puerto Vallarta who was considered a priority target by U.S. authorities. Covarrubias, 41, is wanted on charges of second-degree murder in California.

U.S.-Mexico security coordination continues to deliver results. Through close cooperation between 🇺🇸 & 🇲🇽 authorities, Jalisco Police arrested a fugitive wanted in the United States for murder and other serious crimes. The cooperation advanced by @POTUS @realDonaldTrump and… pic.twitter.com/xVoKAlvceP — Embajador Ronald Johnson (@USAmbMex) August 17, 2026

In a social media post, U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson praised the cooperative effort of Mexican authorities, highlighting the positive results derived from bilateral security coordination.

Illustrating these recent successes, Johnson announced a few hours later that U.S. authorities had “turned over six more fugitives wanted in Mexico for serious crimes, including murder and firearms offenses, with one linked to a narco-terrorist organization.”

The operation in Puerto Vallarta was carried out in coordination with the U.S. Marshals Service after Jalisco authorities received information about the fugitive’s whereabouts in the heart of the popular tourist resort.

With the help of drones and the C2 Mobile Cybertruck, state police and a tactical unit were deployed to the area. According to police reports, Covarrubias was apprehended after a brief chase without incident.

A search of the suspect turned up quantities of marijuana and crystal meth, but charges of drug possession were set aside once it was confirmed that the man was the target sought by U.S. authorities.

State officials contacted the U.S. Marshals Service to begin procedures to hand Covarrubias over for extradition.

On Monday, Ambassador Johnson posted a photograph of the detainee, handcuffed and guarded by four Jalisco police officers, and declared “criminals have nowhere to hide.” The apprehension of Covarrubias is reportedly the ninth arrest of a high-profile U.S. target in the state of Jalisco in recent weeks.

In recent days, U.S. authorities turned over six more fugitives wanted in Mexico for serious crimes, including murder and firearms offenses, with one linked to a narco-terrorist organization. As the cooperation advanced by @POTUS @realDonaldTrump and President @ClaudiaShein… pic.twitter.com/SDhwqeAtIv — Embajador Ronald Johnson (@USAmbMex) August 17, 2026

This spate of captures and extraditions includes the return of three fugitives to Mexico over the weekend. The three suspects — including one who is allegedly a member of the notorious Jalisco New Generation Cartel — were wanted by Mexican authorities on a variety of criminal charges, including murder.

On Sunday, Johnson said the success demonstrates that effective security collaboration sends a clear message to criminals: “You will be caught and you will be held accountable.”

Also last week, the U.S. Marshals Service announced that Mexican authorities had deported one of Texas’ 10 Most Wanted fugitives who was wanted on multiple state and federal charges.

At the same time, Mexican and U.S. authorities conducted a rapid-response binational security exercise along a highly visible stretch of El Paso-Cd. Juárez border area.

With reports from La Jornada, LatinUS, Noticias Puerto Vallarta and Debate

World.title: Sheinbaum says fuel smuggling is ‘over’ in Mexico: Tuesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🇺🇸 Sheinbaum sticks to her “political” reading of AMLO’s son’s visa revocation: Asked whether Andrés Manuel López Beltrán had ever been on authorities’ radar over huachicol fiscal , the president said flatly, “he was not,” and repeated that the cancelation of his U.S. visa is a political matter and a case of “interference in the decisions of Mexico.”

Asked whether Andrés Manuel López Beltrán had ever been on authorities’ radar over , the president said flatly, “he was not,” and repeated that the cancelation of his U.S. visa is a political matter and a case of “interference in the decisions of Mexico.” 🎯 Opposition is using the case to “attack” the government, president says: Because the opposition “has no plan for the country,” Sheinbaum argued, it has seized on the revocation to attack “the project that we represent,” with a barrage of criticism from the right, pundits and media outlets after López Beltrán made the cancelation of his visa public in a letter to U.S. President Donald Trump.

Because the opposition “has no plan for the country,” Sheinbaum argued, it has seized on the revocation to attack “the project that we represent,” with a barrage of criticism from the right, pundits and media outlets after López Beltrán made the cancelation of his visa public in a letter to U.S. President Donald Trump. ⛽ Fuel smuggling “practically over,” according to the president: Sheinbaum said her administration has all but ended huachicol fiscal thanks to interventions in customs and a series of arrests. She complained that government critics ignore that progress in favor of using visa revocations of Morena officials as a political weapon.

Sheinbaum said her administration has all but ended thanks to interventions in customs and a series of arrests. She complained that government critics ignore that progress in favor of using visa revocations of Morena officials as a political weapon. 🚫 “There was no list”: Defending legal adviser Luisa María Alcalde, Sheinbaum denied that a “blacklist” of journalists was presented at last Wednesday’s “right of reply” press conference. She said that Alcalde simply showed how stories from reporters such as Ciro Gómez Leyva, Joaquín López Dóriga, Ana Paula Ordorica, Azucena Uresti and Carlos Loret de Mola are amplified on social media to “create an opinion trend.”

Why today’s mañanera matters

The revocation of the U.S. visa of Andrés Manuel López Beltrán, a son of ex-president Andrés Manuel López Obrador and the former secretary of organization for the ruling Morena party, continues to be a major topic in the national conversation. The revocation came after dozens of other Morena officials, including Baja California Governor Marina del Pilar Ávila, were also stripped of their U.S. visas.

At her Tuesday morning press conference, President Claudia Sheinbaum once again offered her opinion on the situation amid calls from the opposition National Action Party (PAN) for López Beltrán to be investigated for alleged involvement in a tax evasion/fuel smuggling scheme known in Mexico as huachicol fiscal.

Today’s mañanera was also significant as Sheinbaum weighed in on another issue that has received significant attention in recent days. That issue is the presentation by presidential legal adviser Luisa María Alcalde of a list of high-profile journalists and media outlets whose critical coverage of the government is said to be amplified online in order to attack the federal government and the “fourth transformation” political movement that Sheinbaum leads.

Sheinbaum reiterates view that revocation of López Beltrán’s US visa was politically motivated

A reporter noted that the Federal Attorney General’s Office said on Monday that it has no proof that would warrant the commencement of an investigation into allegations that López Beltrán is involved in fuel-related crimes. He asked the president whether López Beltrán was ever on authorities’ “radar” for alleged involvement in huachicol fiscal.

“He was not,” Sheinbaum responded.

“And as I mentioned on Friday, from our point of view this is a political issue,” she said, referring to the revocation of López Beltrán’s U.S. visa.

“It’s not related to other issues,” Sheinbaum said.

Rather, she said, it’s a matter of “interference in the decisions of Mexico.”

“… There are other criminals, or alleged criminals, let’s put it that way, where there is no problem [with their U.S. visas],” Sheinbaum said.

“Or there are other politically exposed persons, as they call them, where it’s the other way around — they open the doors to them,” she said.

“I’m not going to name names because I don’t want to get into a controversy,” Sheinbaum said.

Sheinbaum: Opposition is using revocation of López Beltrán’s visa to ‘attack’ the government

Sheinbaum asserted that “as the opposition has no plan for the country,” it uses the revocation of López Beltrán’s visa to “attack the project that we represent.”

“They take away his visa, he decided to make it public with a letter [addressed to U.S. President Donald Trump] and then the barrage of criticism came from the conservative side of politics, from the right, from the pundits, from the media outlets,” she said.

Sheinbaum: Government has ‘practically’ put an end to huachicol fiscal

Sheinbaum asserted that her administration has “practically” put an end to “huachicol fiscal, or the smuggling of fuel.”

“It’s practically over thanks to the interventions that we’ve been carrying out in customs and the arrests that have been made,” she said.

Sheinbaum said that government critics don’t talk about the progress the government has made in combating huachicol fiscal.

Instead, they use revocations of Morena officials’ U.S. visas to attack the government, she reiterated.

“They have the right to do that. Nobody is going to censor them as they claim we will, but it is necessary to point out the work that has been done [to combat huachicol fiscal],” Sheinbaum said.

Sheinbaum defends her top legal adviser amid claims she disseminated a ‘blacklist’ of journalists

A reporter raised remarks made by Luisa María Alcalde at the “right of reply” press conference she held last Wednesday.

🔴La presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum repitió que “no hubo ninguna lista” de periodistas. Explicó que los nombres de periodistas mencionados por Luisa María Alcalde buscaban mostrar cómo las redes sociales y plataformas digitales pueden amplificar información y generar tendencias de… — Azucena Uresti (@azucenau) August 18, 2026

She asked Sheinbaum whether Alcalde, a former interior minister and national president of Morena, had not “directly blamed” certain journalists for initiating an “offensive” against the government because she said that those journalists are the source of anti-government messages that are subsequently amplified on social media, including by bots.

Alcalde faced significant criticism for presenting a so-called “blacklist” of journalists who are said to be opposed to the federal government. In addition, video footage of Sheinbaum saying in 2021 that the drawing up of lists of political adversaries is a practice of McCarthyism and Nazism was widely shared on social media.

On Tuesday morning, Sheinbaum asserted that Alcalde did not in fact present a list at her “right of reply” press conference, a relatively new initiative of the federal government.

“First, there was no list,” she said.

“Names were presented — what Luisa presented … what she showed is the use of digital platforms, of social media, to amplify a piece of news and even create fake news,” Sheinbaum said.

“That’s what she presented,” she said.

Sheinbaum said that Alcalde showed how “a piece of news from these journalists” — among whom were Ciro Gómez Leyva, Joaquín López Dóriga, Ana Paula Ordorica, Azucena Uresti and Carlos Loret de Mola —can be amplified on social media to “create an opinion trend.”

“There are multiple cases of this that we can talk about, many cases,” she said. Narco-government, narco-candidate, narco-president, all that,” Sheinbaum said.

The president went on to say that her government defends the right to free speech.

“Who here has been censored? Give me the name of a journalist we’ve censored,” Sheinbaum said.

“There isn’t one. Tell me the name of a media outlet we’ve censored. There isn’t one,” she said.

Key Facts —The award: O Melhor de São Paulo Gastronomia 2026, Folha’s fifteenth edition. —Announced: Monday 17 August 2026, at the Sala São Paulo. —Jury winners: 43, chosen by 45 journalists and content producers. —Public winners: 20 more, from a Datafolha survey of São Paulo residents. —First award of the night: Tordesilhas, the restaurant run by chef Mara Salles. —Bars: Bar do Luiz Fernandes took three Datafolha categories at once.

Forty-three winners picked by a jury of forty-five, twenty more picked by the city itself, and a 260-page guide behind them. The ceremony was Monday night.

Folha de S.Paulo announced the winners of its 2026 dining awards at the Sala São Paulo on Monday 17 August. It is the fifteenth edition of the guide behind them.

Folha’s 2026 São Paulo awards split between a jury of 45 and a Datafolha survey of residents. Bar do Luiz Fernandes took three public categories. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

How the São Paulo awards work

There are two sets of winners, decided in two different ways. A jury of 45 journalists and content producers chose 43 of them.

The categories run wide. They cover best restaurant, cocktail bar, bakery, patisserie and ice cream shop, plus chef, sommelier and barista of the year.

Separately, Datafolha surveyed São Paulo residents and produced 20 more winners. Those are the houses the city itself named, which is a different measure entirely.

Neither set is a ranking. Both are lists of winners by category, which is a different thing from an order of merit.

The night’s first award

The first prize handed out went to Tordesilhas, the restaurant run by chef Mara Salles. Folha described it as a house that came to stand for the case for Brazilian cooking in São Paulo.

That order of ceremony is a statement in itself. It puts a Brazilian kitchen at the front of a city better known for its Italian and Japanese cooking.

What the public picked

Bar do Luiz Fernandes, in the northern zone, took three Datafolha categories. They were best boteco, best bar to eat at and best beer list.

A boteco is the neighbourhood bar that serves food, closer to a corner pub than a restaurant. It is the most São Paulo category on the list.

Bar Brahma tied on the beer list category. Another house took best bar for the small hours.

A city with no single answer

One figure in Folha’s coverage says more than any winner. In the best-restaurant category, houses reaching one percent of spontaneous mentions rose from 21 in 2012 to 28 in 2026.

The field is spreading rather than concentrating. There is no consensus best restaurant in São Paulo, and the data now shows it.

What a São Paulo boteco is

The boteco is the format the city is built on. It is a bar with a kitchen, tiled floors, cold beer and plates meant for sharing.

It is not a tourist category. A good boteco is where a São Paulo neighbourhood eats on a weekday.

The guide behind the awards

The awards sit inside a 260-page special, O Melhor de São Paulo Gastronomia — Restaurantes, Bares e Cozinha 2026.

It also carries a separate feature listing 43 bars that serve good petiscos and full dishes. Petiscos are the small plates that a São Paulo bar lives on.

The two lists of 43 are different things in the same publication, and should not be read as one.

Fifteen editions makes this the longest-running dining award in the city. That continuity is most of its authority.

Why this matters if you have just arrived

São Paulo has more restaurants than any visitor can navigate, and the recommendations you get depend entirely on who you ask.

A jury list and a public poll disagreeing with each other is more useful than either alone. Between them they cover the room you want on a Tuesday and the one you book for a birthday.

Read the Datafolha list for where people actually go. Read the jury list for what the trade rates.

A corner grill in Palermo has held the top place on the world steak ranking for three consecutive years. Tables go two to three weeks out.

Don Julio sits on the corner of Gurruchaga and Guatemala in Palermo Viejo, behind pink walls and wooden windows. It has been named the world’s best steak restaurant three years running.

What Don Julio is

It is a parrilla, the Argentine grill house built around a wood or charcoal fire and a rack of beef cuts. The format is ordinary in Buenos Aires; the execution here is not.

The restaurant occupies a corner site in Palermo Viejo, with pink walls and wooden window frames. Expansión described it on 17 August as a classic-looking room.

Pablo Rivero owns it. He came to the business as a sommelier, which is unusual for a grill and shows in the wine list.

Don Julio dry-ages its beef and works with named producers. That is what separates it from the hundreds of other grills in this city.

The award it actually holds

Don Julio has been named best steak restaurant in the world for three consecutive years. The ranking is the World’s 101 Best Steak Restaurants.

That is the current, live accolade, and it is specific to beef rather than to restaurants in general.

Three years at the top of a single-subject ranking says more about consistency than a one-off placing would.

Where it stands on the wider lists

Don Julio placed 10th in The World’s 50 Best Restaurants in 2025. That is the most recent edition of that list.

The 2026 ranking has not been published. It will be revealed in Lima on 4 November, the first South American ceremony in the list’s 24-year history.

Any 2026 position for Don Julio is therefore still unknown, whatever the tourist pages say.

What it costs

Expansión put the à la carte spend at €100 to €150 a head on 17 August. It noted that a firm average is hard to fix because the peso moves.

That is the figure as published, in euros. Argentine restaurant prices in pesos change often enough that a converted number would be out of date before it was read.

Getting a table

Reservations go through the website or by WhatsApp. Two to three weeks ahead is the guidance for landing a specific date.

Demand is steady rather than seasonal. Booking from abroad before you fly is the sensible approach.

Walk-ins are possible but the wait can be long. The bar next door takes the overflow, which is part of the ritual.

Palermo Viejo, around Don Julio

The neighbourhood is Buenos Aires at its most walkable, with low buildings, jacaranda and a bar on most corners.

It is also where most visitors stay. Don Julio is not a trek from anywhere in the district.

What a parrilla actually serves

The cuts a visitor will meet first are bife de chorizo, a sirloin, and ojo de bife, the ribeye. Entraña is skirt steak and vacío is flank.

Asado de tira is short rib cut across the bone. Chinchulines and mollejas, intestine and sweetbreads, open most traditional meals.

Ordering a steak beyond medium is possible everywhere and welcomed almost nowhere. Jugoso means rare, a punto medium.

Chimichurri arrives on the table by default. It is a herb and vinegar sauce, not a marinade, and it goes on after the meat is cooked.

World.title: Bahia’s Moqueca and Bobó Rank in the World’s Top 20 Seafood Dishes
World.content:

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

Bahia · FOOD & DRINK

Key Facts —The list: TasteAtlas, World’s 100 Most Iconic Seafood Dishes, published August 2026. —Moqueca baiana: 16th, a fish stew in coconut milk and palm oil. —Bobó de camarão: 17th, shrimp in a cassava and coconut purée. —:Both are Bahian, and both are built on azeite de dendê, palm oil. —:The list ranks dishes, not restaurants, and names no kitchen. —Where to eat them: Casa de Tereza, chef Tereza Paim, in Rio Vermelho, Salvador.

Two dishes from the same kitchen tradition landed inside the top twenty of a global list. Both come out of Bahia, and both start with palm oil.

TasteAtlas placed moqueca baiana at number 16 and bobó de camarão at 17. The list, of the world’s 100 most iconic seafood dishes, went out in mid-August.

Moqueca baiana ranked 16th and bobó de camarão 17th on TasteAtlas’s list of the world’s 100 most iconic seafood dishes. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What the ranking actually says

TasteAtlas, the food and travel guide, published its list of the world’s 100 most iconic seafood dishes this month. Two Bahian entries landed side by side.

Moqueca baiana came in at 16 and bobó de camarão at 17. Brazilian coverage of the list ran on 13 August.

One thing to be clear about: the list ranks dishes, not restaurants. TasteAtlas does not name a kitchen alongside either entry.

Both dishes come from the same kitchen tradition and the same coastline. Neither is a national dish; both are unmistakably Bahian.

What moqueca baiana is

It is a fish stew simmered in coconut milk and azeite de dendê, with tomatoes and peppers. Dendê is the orange palm oil of Bahian cooking.

It arrives bubbling in the clay pot it was cooked in. That pot, the panela de barro, is part of the dish rather than a presentation choice.

Moqueca is the plate that carries Bahia’s Afro-Brazilian kitchen to the rest of the country.

Moqueca has a rival version in Espírito Santo, made without palm oil or coconut milk. Bahians and capixabas have argued about it for a century.

And what bobó de camarão is

Shrimp simmered into a creamy purée of cassava root, coconut milk and dendê oil. It is thicker and starchier than moqueca, and closer to its cousin vatapá.

The base starts with onion, garlic, tomato and bell peppers softened in oil. Coconut milk goes in, then the shrimp and the cassava cream.

It is finished with more dendê and fresh coriander. Cassava, called mandioca or aipim depending on where you are, does the work that cream would do elsewhere.

The difference, in one line

Moqueca is a stew you eat with a spoon and rice. Bobó is closer to a purée, and it holds its shape on the plate.

Both use the same three foundations: coconut milk, palm oil and the peppers. What changes is the body.

Order both on the same table if there are two of you. Side by side is the fastest way to understand the difference.

Where to eat them in Salvador

Bahian coverage of the ranking pointed at Casa de Tereza. The restaurant is run by chef Tereza Paim in the Rio Vermelho district of Salvador.

Both dishes are on its menu, and the restaurant is closely associated with them. Its full street address has not been published in the coverage we checked.

Rio Vermelho is Salvador’s eating and nightlife district, on the coast north of Barra.

Salvador is not short of places serving moqueca. What the coverage singled out was one kitchen closely tied to both dishes at once.

A note on dendê

Azeite de dendê is unrefined palm oil, and it is the single ingredient that makes Bahian food taste the way it does. It is heavy, and it is not subtle.

Visitors who find it too rich sometimes ask for a version without it. In moqueca that is a different dish, and most kitchens in Salvador will say so.

Rio Vermelho also has the acarajé stands that Salvador is known for. Dendê runs through those too.

What else made the list

The list runs to a hundred dishes from around the world. Two Brazilian entries inside the top twenty is a strong showing for one regional kitchen.

TasteAtlas has not published a methodology note alongside this ranking, so treat the order as a guide rather than a verdict.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where did moqueca and bobó de camarão rank? TasteAtlas placed moqueca baiana at number 16 and bobó de camarão at number 17. The list of the world’s 100 most iconic seafood dishes was published in August 2026. What is the difference between moqueca and bobó de camarão? Moqueca is a fish stew simmered in coconut milk and palm oil and served in a clay pot. Bobó is shrimp in a thicker purée of cassava, coconut milk and palm oil. Did a restaurant win the ranking? No. The list ranks dishes rather than restaurants, and names no kitchen. Bahian coverage pointed readers to Casa de Tereza, run by chef Tereza Paim in Rio Vermelho, Salvador. What is azeite de dendê? It is unrefined palm oil, deep orange and strongly flavoured. It is the defining ingredient of Bahian cooking and appears in both dishes.

World.title: A Belo Horizonte Coffee School Reopens Today, Three Times Bigger

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

Belo Horizonte · FOOD & DRINK

Key Facts —Academia do Café: now at Rua Grão Pará 1010, Funcionários, Belo Horizonte. —Opens: Tuesday 18 August 2026, in a house three times larger. —Hours: every day, 9am to 6pm. —Coffee: espresso from R$9.50, about US$1.83. —Food: house-made toasts and pastries, R$16 to R$32, roughly US$3 to US$6. —Also on site: a coffee counter, a roastery and an experience room.

The café and coffee school has moved into a house three times the size of the old one, on the same street. The menu changed with the address.

Academia do Café reopens on Tuesday 18 August at Rua Grão Pará 1010, in the Funcionários district of Belo Horizonte. The new house is three times the size of the old one.

Academia do Café reopens on Rua Grão Pará in Belo Horizonte with a house three times larger. An espresso is R$9.50, about US$1.83. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What Academia do Café has become

The move is a few doors along the same street, but the difference is scale. The new house is three times the size of the one it replaces.

It now works as four things at once: a café, a coffee school, a roastery and a room built for tastings. The owners describe the extra space as the point of the move.

A dedicated counter has been given over to coffee preparation, which is what the school teaches.

Academia do Café has not gone far. The old address was on the same street, which keeps the regulars it built there.

The new menu

The drinks list has widened. A simple espresso is R$9.50, about US$1.83 at the rate of R$5.2012 to the dollar quoted on 17 August.

An italian cappuccino is R$15, a shakerato R$18, the house mocha R$26 and an orange brew with strawberry R$28. That last pair sit around US$5.

The kitchen is new. Toasts on naturally leavened bread come with mushrooms and spices at R$28, roasted peppers at R$32 or creamed chicken at R$32.

A grilled brioche cheese sandwich is R$28. A ham and cheese roll in potato-bread dough is R$16, and a creamy corn broa the same.

Everything on the food side is now made in house. That is the substantive change, more than the address.

For the sweet end

A chocolate and cashew brownie is R$18, a cheese and guava tart R$24, and cream doughnuts R$10, which is under US$2.

Guava and cheese together is the Brazilian pairing known as Romeu e Julieta. It is a Minas Gerais staple rather than an invention of the house.

Prices sit where a good independent café in Brazil sits. Nothing on the list breaks US$7.

Where it is, and when to go

Funcionários is a central district of Belo Horizonte, next to Savassi and walkable from most of the city-centre hotels.

The café opens seven days a week, from 9am to 6pm. That is a daytime business rather than an evening one.

It is a short walk from the Praça da Liberdade museums. That makes it a plausible stop rather than a detour.

What a café and school does differently

Most cafés sell you a coffee. This one also teaches you to make it, in a room built for the purpose.

For a foreign resident, that is the practical difference. The counter staff expect questions about method, and answer them.

Why a coffee school matters here

Minas Gerais grows more coffee than any other Brazilian state. A large share of what the country exports comes from its hills.

A school attached to a café in the state capital is closer to the source than almost any equivalent elsewhere. The courses are part of the business, not a sideline.

Academia do Café sells the roast as well as the cup. The roastery is part of the new building.

The courses were the reason for the bigger house, so a schedule is likely to follow shortly.

What has not been announced

Course dates and prices for the school have not been published alongside the reopening.

The full previous address has not been given either, beyond the fact that the old site was on the same street.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where is Academia do Café now? At Rua Grão Pará 1010, in the Funcionários district of Belo Horizonte, Minas Gerais. The new house is three times the size of the previous one on the same street. When does it open? The new site opens on Tuesday 18 August 2026, and trades every day from 9am to 6pm. What does coffee cost there? A simple espresso is R$9.50, about US$1.83. A cappuccino is R$15, a shakerato R$18 and the house mocha R$26, which is around US$5. Is there food as well as coffee? Yes. The kitchen makes toasts on naturally leavened bread from R$28 to R$32. Pastries and cakes start at R$10.

World.title: Tolima Wildfires Scorch 11,000 Hectares in Central Colombia
World.content:
Colombia · Security

Key Facts — The count Tolima had 17 active fires and more than 11,000 hectares affected on 18 August, per the department’s environment and risk office.

— The declaration Tolima’s departmental risk council declared a public calamity on 14 August, when close to 39 fires were burning.

— The worst hit official tallies put Ortega at 3,185 hectares, Rovira at 1,814 and Honda at 1,080; San Luis’s mayor says his municipality alone lost over 7,500.

— The weather IDEAM links a strengthening El Nino to the heat and rain deficit, with roughly 340 municipalities on red fire alert nationwide.

— The other emergency the military says its 11 August operation in Catatumbo killed two ELN fighters; the ombudsman says three farmers were hurt.

Tolima has lost more land to fire this month than Colombia recorded nationwide in the seven weeks to 6 August.

Illustrative photo: blackened ground and dry grass beside a highway after a forest fire. Colombia’s Tolima department reported 17 active fires and more than 11,000 hectares affected on 18 August 2026. (Photo: Jose Joaquin Cortes, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

Seventeen Tolima wildfires were still burning on Tuesday, and more than 11,000 hectares of central Colombian countryside have gone with them. Tolima is a farming department of about 47 municipalities, west of Bogota.

Its risk council declared a public calamity on 14 August, and the fires have not stopped since.

What the Tolima Wildfires Have Burned So Far

El Colombiano reported on 18 August that Tolima still had 17 active fires. The figure came from the department’s environment and risk management office.

That same office put the burned area at more than 11,000 hectares. Infobae, working from a later balance, said the total had already passed 11,700.

How the Emergency Escalated

The trouble built through early August. Caracol Radio counted just over 1,700 hectares burned in Tolima on 8 August.

Six days later the department was fighting close to 39 fires at once. That is why the risk council declared a public calamity on 14 August.

Where the Flames Hit Hardest

The official municipal breakdown, published by Caracol Radio, is led by Ortega with 3,185 hectares. Rovira follows with 1,814, then Honda with 1,080 and Coello with 600.

San Luis sits high on that list too, although its numbers are disputed. Valle de San Juan, Guamo, Melgar and Chaparral have all reported active fronts.

The Numbers Are Still Moving

Consolidated figures lag the fire. The mayor of San Luis, Ricardo Andres Acosta, told Caracol that firefighters measured over 7,500 hectares burned in his municipality alone.

The departmental table gives San Luis a far smaller share. Until surveys are finished, the honest reading is that the official total is a floor, not a ceiling.

Why Tolima Is So Dry

June to August is normally a dry stretch in much of Colombia. This year, however, the state weather agency IDEAM says a strengthening El Nino is sharpening it.

IDEAM’s August climate bulletin forecasts below-normal rainfall across the Andean and Caribbean regions. It also issued heat-wave notices naming Tolima among the hottest areas.

What Started the Fires

No single confirmed ignition cause has been published for the Tolima cluster. Authorities point to heat, drought and dry vegetation as the conditions that let small fires run.

Burning of pasture and other human activity is often blamed in Colombia’s fire seasons. Even so, no arson case or arrest tied to these particular fires has been confirmed.

The Response on the Ground

Governor Adriana Magali Matiz has coordinated the response since the calamity declaration. Firefighters, soldiers and environmental staff are working the fronts, backed by aircraft.

A police Black Hawk and a Colombian Aerospace Force helicopter have flown water drops. The governor also contracted extra aircraft for the worst points, including San Luis.

Colombia’s Wider Fire Season

This is not only a Tolima problem. National reporting on 14 August put about 340 municipalities on red alert for forest fires, roughly double the previous day’s count.

The national disaster agency UNGRD logged 438 forest fires across 191 municipalities between 16 June and 6 August. Those fires affected about 7,153 hectares, far less than Tolima has lost since.

The Second Emergency: Catatumbo

Catatumbo is a rugged, coca-growing region of Norte de Santander, on the Venezuelan border. It has been the front line of Colombia’s fight with the ELN guerrilla group since January 2025.

President Abelardo de la Espriella took office on 7 August and scrapped his predecessor’s ‘total peace’ policy. His defence minister, retired general Jorge Eduardo Mora Lopez, has promised a sustained military and police campaign there.

What the Military Says It Achieved

The armed forces say an operation codenamed Beta hit ELN structures in rural Tibu and San Calixto early on 11 August. They claim two suspected members killed, five camps destroyed and two bunkers wrecked.

Mora said troops seized 1.5 tonnes of explosives, enough, he argued, to arm up to 3,000 drones. These are military claims, and independent verification is limited.

The Civilian Cost, According to the Ombudsman

Colombia’s ombudsman, the Defensoria del Pueblo, says three farmers were injured in the operation’s area. It has asked prosecutors to establish who is responsible.

The defence ministry denies that its strike harmed civilians. The ombudsman also flagged other incidents in the same week.

Six people were hurt by an explosive dropped from a drone in rural Sardinata. An elderly man was maimed by a landmine near Tibu.

Retaliation on the Cucuta Road

On 17 August three police officers were seized on the Cucuta-Ocana road, in Bucarasica. The defence ministry called it retaliation by illegal armed groups for recent operations.

No group had publicly claimed the officers by 18 August, and there was no confirmation of their release. Search operations were still running.

A Displacement Crisis That Never Ended

The current fighting sits on top of an older wound. After the January 2025 escalation, UN humanitarians recorded 77,418 people affected in eight Catatumbo municipalities.

Of those, 51,938 were forced from their homes, in what OCHA called the region’s largest mass displacement in 28 years. Human Rights Watch later cited more than 64,000 displaced and over 137,000 confined between January and August 2025.

What to Watch Next

Rain arrived in parts of Tolima on 17 August, and the governor welcomed it publicly. Still, IDEAM’s outlook keeps rainfall below normal into October, so relief may be brief.

In Catatumbo, the tests are simpler and harder. Whether the three officers come home, and whether the ombudsman’s civilian-harm findings go anywhere, will say more than any operation tally.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many Tolima wildfires are still burning?

Tolima’s environment and risk office reported 17 active fires on 18 August 2026. That is down from close to 39 when the public calamity was declared on 14 August.

How much land has burned in Tolima?

More than 11,000 hectares, per the departmental figures cited on 18 August. A later balance reported by Infobae put the total above 11,700 hectares, and surveys are still being completed.

Is El Nino to blame?

IDEAM says El Nino conditions are present and strengthening, deepening the normal mid-year dry season. It has forecast below-normal rain and issued heat-wave notices covering Tolima.

What is happening in Catatumbo?

The military is running an offensive against the ELN in Norte de Santander. It claims results from an 11 August operation, while the ombudsman reports civilian injuries.

Sources: El Colombiano; Caracol Radio; Infobae; EFE; IDEAM; UNGRD; UN OCHA; Human Rights Watch.

World.title: Where Your Salary Goes Furthest: Buenos Aires, Montevideo or Santiago
World.content:
Southern Cone · Cost of Living

Key Facts The reference pay Argentina, median gross of 1,600,829 pesos a month (about US$1,075); Uruguay, average gross of 34,600 pesos (about US$864); Chile, average gross of 1,333,905 pesos (about US$1,459).

Argentina, median gross of 1,600,829 pesos a month (about US$1,075); Uruguay, average gross of 34,600 pesos (about US$864); Chile, average gross of 1,333,905 pesos (about US$1,459). The rent A two-room flat in a mid-range district: 860,000 pesos in Buenos Aires (about US$578), 20,500 in Montevideo (about US$512), 652,000 in Santiago (about US$713).

A two-room flat in a mid-range district: 860,000 pesos in Buenos Aires (about US$578), 20,500 in Montevideo (about US$512), 652,000 in Santiago (about US$713). As a share of pay That is 54% of the reference wage in Buenos Aires, 59% in Montevideo and 49% in Santiago.

That is 54% of the reference wage in Buenos Aires, 59% in Montevideo and 49% in Santiago. If you earn in dollars Montevideo is the cheapest of the three to rent in, not Buenos Aires. Santiago is the dearest, by roughly US$200 a month.

Montevideo is the cheapest of the three to rent in, not Buenos Aires. Santiago is the dearest, by roughly US$200 a month. The equipment gap A mid-range laptop costs 111% of a month’s gross pay in Argentina, 80% in Uruguay and 49% in Chile — and Randstad says that persists despite recent tariff cuts.

A mid-range laptop costs 111% of a month’s gross pay in Argentina, 80% in Uruguay and 49% in Chile — and Randstad says that persists despite recent tariff cuts. Two numbers to distrust Randstad’s own Chilean wage estimate more than doubled in two years, and its Uruguayan average sits below the entry-level Montevideo salary quoted in the same document.

A staffing firm has just compared what a salary buys in the three southern-cone capitals. The answer is useful — but only once you know which of its numbers to trust.

If you are choosing between the three capitals of the southern cone, someone has finally done the arithmetic for you. Randstad, the staffing group, published a comparison on 5 August of what a local salary buys in Buenos Aires, Montevideo and Santiago. It is worth reading. It is also worth checking, because two of its headline findings come apart when you hold them against the national statistics offices — and the cost-of-living comparison between Buenos Aires, Montevideo and Santiago that survives is a different one from the one making the rounds.

A two-room flat in a mid-range Montevideo district runs about US$512 a month — the cheapest of the three capitals. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

RT Ask Rio Times Straight answers about living in Argentina, from our reporting. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times → RT Ask Rio TimesCost of living, safety, visas in Argentina › RT Ask Rio Times Straight answers about living in Argentina, from our reporting. × Cost of living Is it safe? Visas Neighborhoods Tap a question, or type your own — the answer appears right here. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

What the cost of living in Buenos Aires, Montevideo and Santiago actually looks like

Randstad divides a capital-city rent by a national wage figure and reports the share. On that measure Santiago looks lightest at 49%, Buenos Aires sits at 54% and Montevideo is heaviest at 59%.

The laptop comparison is the one that really separates the three. A mainstream machine — an i5 processor, 16 GB of memory, a 500 GB solid-state drive — costs about 1.8 million pesos in Argentina, which is 111% of the monthly reference wage. The same machine is 80% of a month’s pay in Uruguay and 49% in Chile. Randstad is explicit that the gap has survived the tax and tariff changes of recent years, so this is not simply an import-duty story any more.

Home internet follows the same order: 2.5% of the reference wage in Argentina, 2.38% in Uruguay, 0.75% in Chile. So does a Big Mac and so does a litre of regular petrol. On every everyday item, Santiago is cheapest relative to local pay, Buenos Aires is in the middle and Montevideo is dearest.

The number that changed is Randstad’s, not the market’s

The finding being repeated everywhere is that Santiago has flipped from the most expensive of the three to the least, falling from 64% of a wage two years ago to 49% now. That reads as a housing story. It is not one.

Santiago rents in Randstad’s own figures rose 63% over those two years, from 400,000 to 652,000 pesos. What fell was the denominator’s grip: Randstad’s Chilean reference wage went from 625,000 pesos to 1,333,905, a rise of 113% in a period when Chilean consumer prices rose by well under a tenth of that. Both figures are labelled in the documents as Randstad Chile’s own estimate.

Chile’s national statistics institute published its 2025 income survey in July. It puts average monthly labour income at 962,945 pesos, and the average for private-sector employees at 1,019,104. Divide Randstad’s 652,000 rent by that private-sector average and you get 64% — precisely where Randstad had Santiago two years ago.

So the honest version is: on the official income data, Santiago has not become the affordable one. Randstad revised its own estimate.

The Uruguayan wage does not hold up either

Randstad puts Uruguay’s average gross private-sector pay at 34,600 pesos a month. Four things sit awkwardly against that.

Its own 2024 edition said 58,075 — a 40% nominal fall in two years, in a country where the wage index has been rising about 5% a year. Uruguay’s minimum wage is 25,383 pesos, so an average of 34,600 would put the typical worker at 1.36 times the floor. And in the same 2026 document, Randstad quotes a Montevideo administrative employee’s starting gross at 35,000 pesos — higher than the national average it reports.

Because the Montevideo rent figure was cut by almost exactly the same proportion, the 59% ratio survives. Treat the ratio as indicative and the underlying pesos with care.

What actually holds, and what it means for you

Two things in the study are solid, and they are the two most useful to anyone deciding where to live.

The first is the equipment gap, and it is enormous. If your income depends on a working laptop and a working connection, Argentina charges you more than a month’s local pay for the machine and Chile charges you half that. For a remote worker replacing hardware every few years, that is a real and repeating cost, not a rounding error.

The second is the absolute rent, which matters more than any ratio if you are paid in dollars. Montevideo is the cheapest of the three at about US$512, Buenos Aires next at about US$578, and Santiago the most expensive at about US$713. That is the reverse of the ratio ranking, and it is the number that decides your month if your income does not come in pesos.

One caveat applies to all of it. Randstad divides capital-city rents by national wage figures, and all three capitals pay above their national averages. Every percentage in the study therefore overstates the burden on someone who actually lives in the city. And the Argentine wage is April 2026 data reported in July, so it lags a nominal reality that has moved since.

Reading the currency

The dollar figures here are converted at the rates prevailing on 18 August 2026: about 1,489 pesos to the dollar wholesale in Argentina, 40.05 in Uruguay and 914 in Chile.

The Argentine number needs one note. The gap between the official and parallel rates, which used to make any dollar comparison meaningless, is now about two per cent — the parallel rate is around 1,525 to 1,545. At that rate the Argentine figures come out roughly 4% cheaper in dollars, which does not change any of the rankings above.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which of the three cities is cheapest to rent in? In absolute dollars, Montevideo, at about US$512 a month for a two-room flat in a mid-range district, against about US$578 in Buenos Aires and about US$713 in Santiago. As a share of local pay the order reverses: Santiago is lightest at 49%, then Buenos Aires at 54%, then Montevideo at 59%. Has Santiago really become more affordable? Not on the official data. The fall from 64% to 49% of a wage comes from Randstad more than doubling its own Chilean wage estimate. Using Chile’s national statistics institute figure for average private-sector pay, Santiago’s rent is still about 64% of income. Why is a laptop so much more expensive in Argentina? It costs about 111% of a month’s gross reference pay in Argentina, against 80% in Uruguay and 49% in Chile. Randstad notes the gap has persisted despite the tax and tariff changes of recent years, so it is no longer only about import duties. Are the wage figures comparable across the three countries? Not exactly. The Argentine figure is a median gross wage from the labour secretariat’s SIPA report; the Uruguayan and Chilean figures are Randstad’s own estimates of an average. Medians and averages are not the same measure, and the study mixes them. Which exchange rate do these dollar figures use? The rates of 18 August 2026 — about 1,489 Argentine pesos, 40.05 Uruguayan pesos and 914 Chilean pesos to the dollar. Argentina’s parallel rate is about two per cent above the official one, which shifts the Argentine figures roughly 4% without changing any ranking. When was the study published? Randstad published it on 5 August 2026. An earlier edition, used here for the two-year comparison, was published on 1 August 2024.

Sources: Randstad — living and working in Montevideo, Santiago or Bue; INE Chile — Encuesta Suplementaria de Ingresos; El Cronista — where the salary goes furthest; El Observador — the salary and cost-of-living gap

World.title: Chinese Cars in Mexico Hit 17% of Sales Despite a 50% Tariff
World.content:
Mexico · Business

Key Facts — The share Chinese brands took 17% of Mexico’s new light-vehicle sales in the first half of 2026, up from 14% a year earlier, according to dealer association AMDA.

— The volume Those brands sold 137,525 vehicles from January to June, against 107,712 in the same months of 2025.

— The tariff A 50% duty on cars from countries without a trade deal with Mexico took effect on 1 January 2026. It is law, not a proposal.

— The origin shift Counting every badge, roughly 22% of vehicles sold in Mexico this year were built in China, making China the number two supplier after Mexico itself.

— The workweek Mexico’s move to a 40-hour week is enacted, but the first cut, from 48 to 46 hours, only starts on 1 January 2027.

China is now the second-largest source of the vehicles Mexicans buy, behind only Mexico’s own assembly lines.

Illustrative photo: a BYD Seagull compact electric hatchback. BYD sold 33,969 vehicles in Mexico in the first half of 2026, still the largest Chinese brand in the market. (Photo: User3204, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

Chinese cars in Mexico are selling faster than the tariff meant to slow them. Chinese brands took 17% of the country’s new light-vehicle market in the first half of 2026, up from 14% a year earlier.

That happened even though a 50% import duty has been in force since January.

How Far Chinese Cars in Mexico Have Come

The dealer association AMDA counted 137,525 vehicles from Chinese brands between January and June. A year earlier the figure was 107,712, so the jump is close to 28%.

Four years ago Chinese cars in Mexico were a curiosity on the road. Since then these brands have moved from roughly 7% of the market to 17%, and the climb has not paused.

The 50% Tariff Is Already Law

This is the part that is often reported wrongly. Mexico’s Senate approved the tariff package on 11 December 2025.

The decree was published days later, and it took effect on 1 January 2026. The measure raised duties on 1,463 tariff lines covering goods from countries that have no free-trade agreement with Mexico.

Cars carry the top rate of 50%, whether they run on petrol, diesel or a battery.

Why the Duty Has Not Stopped the Advance

The tariff clearly bit at the border. Imports of Chinese light vehicles fell about 43% by value in the first five months of 2026 compared with the year before.

Yet showroom sales kept rising, because importers had shipped heavily before the deadline and are still working through that stock. Brands have also absorbed part of the cost rather than pass it all to buyers.

Which Brands Are Actually Winning

BYD remains the biggest Chinese name in Mexico, with 33,969 units in the first half. Interestingly, that was slightly below the 34,606 it sold a year earlier.

MG has been the momentum story instead. It moved 32,013 vehicles from January to July, a 16% annual gain.

For a 3.6% national share and eighth place among all brands. Chirey, Geely, Changan and Great Wall fill out the rest of the pack.

China Is Now Mexico’s Number Two Car Supplier

Look at where cars are built rather than whose badge they wear, and the picture is starker. Mexican plants supplied about 32% of the vehicles sold at home in the first half.

China came second at roughly 22%, ahead of Brazil, India, the United States and Japan. In short, a Chinese factory is now behind about one in five new cars sold in Mexico.

Why the Numbers Do Not Always Match

Readers will see several different percentages, and there is a reason. Some Chinese brands do not report their sales to the statistics agency INEGI, so official tallies undercount them.

AMDA said in August that reporting Chinese brands held 11.5% of the January-to-July market. Adding the brands that stay silent lifts that to about 17%, and counting every China-built vehicle pushes it toward 28%.

What President Sheinbaum Has Said

President Claudia Sheinbaum defended the duty when it was still a proposal in September 2025. She said the measures were not aimed at Beijing, calling them decisions taken with every country Mexico has no trade deal with.

She framed the plan as industrial policy rather than diplomacy, denying it was a concession to Washington. Since the decree took effect, her government has treated the 50% rate as settled policy, not as something still under review.

A Record Market Is Softening the Blow

Mexico sold 885,349 new light vehicles from January to July, up 5% year on year. That is the strongest seven-month stretch since the official series began in 2005.

A growing market makes room for newcomers without forcing anyone out. As a result, established brands have lost share while still selling more cars than before.

The 40-Hour Week Arrives Next

Separately, Mexico has locked in a shorter working week. The constitutional change was published on 3 March 2026 and the labour-law rewrite followed on 1 May 2026.

The reduction is gradual rather than immediate. The legal maximum stays at 48 hours through 2026, then falls to 46 hours in 2027.

44 in 2028, 42 in 2029 and 40 in 2030.

Factories Are Redrawing Shifts, Not Hiring

Employers are reaching for the schedule before the payroll. A WTW survey reported in late July found that about 70% of companies plan to adjust working hours to absorb the change.

Consultants describe the same instinct: compress the week, rotate shifts, lean on automation, and hire only as a last resort. EY has estimated payroll costs could rise 15% to 20% for firms that choose to add staff instead.

Most Companies Are Not Ready

Preparation is thin. A survey published on 6 August found only 17.8% of Mexican firms feel fully ready for the January 2027 cut in hours.

An earlier EY study put it more bluntly, reporting that 72% had taken no concrete step at all. Because the first reduction is small, many managers appear to be treating it as a 2027 problem.

What to Watch Next

Two things will decide whether Chinese cars in Mexico hold their gains. The first is inventory: once pre-tariff stock runs out, sticker prices will show the duty more honestly.

The second is assembly inside Mexico, which would sidestep the tariff altogether. Meanwhile, the shift math starts for real in January 2027.

And factories that have not planned for it will feel the squeeze first.

Frequently Asked Questions

What share of Mexico’s car market do Chinese brands hold?

Chinese brands took 17% of new light-vehicle sales in the first half of 2026. Up from 14% a year earlier, according to the dealer association AMDA.

Has Mexico actually imposed tariffs on Chinese cars?

Yes. Congress approved the package in December 2025 and it took effect on 1 January 2026.

Which Chinese car brands sell most in Mexico?

BYD led the first half with 33,969 units. MG sold 32,013 from January to July for a 3.6% national share, with Chirey, Geely, Changan and Great Wall also present.

When does Mexico’s 40-hour workweek start?

The law is already enacted, but the phase-in begins on 1 January 2027 at 46 hours. It falls two hours a year until it reaches 40 hours in 2030.

Sources: Reuters; AMDA; INEGI; El Economista; Diario Oficial de la Federacion.

World.title: Argentina Imports of Consumer Goods Hit a Record US$5.4 Billion
World.content:
Argentina · Economy

Key Facts — The record Consumer-goods imports reached US$5.36 billion in the first half of 2026, the highest ever for a January-June period, according to a CEPA report published on 17 August.

— The share Consumer goods made up 15.1% of all imports, the biggest slice in 22 years. Against the first half of 2023, the total rose 34.7%.

— The 500% line Imported pasta rose 530.8% and meat 315.2%. However, those figures compare 2026 with 2023, not with last year.

— The peso The wholesale dollar closed at ARS 1,487.50 on 14 August, roughly 25% below the ceiling of the central bank’s currency band.

— The credit switch From 14 August, banks may lend up to 15% of their dollar deposits to companies that earn no foreign currency.

The number of firms bringing consumer goods into the country has doubled since 2023, and imported pasta is up more than 500%.

Shipping containers and imported vehicles on racks at a South American container terminal. Illustrative photo. Argentina’s consumer-goods imports reached a record US$5.36 billion in the first half of 2026. (Photo: Claudio Elias, Public domain, Wikimedia Commons.)
