World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018892/‘Just So Easy’: Why China’s Gen Z Prefers Credit Without the Card
World.title: ‘Just So Easy’: Why China’s Gen Z Prefers Credit Without the Card
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018892/‘Just So Easy’: Why China’s Gen Z Prefers Credit Without the Card
World.content:
Yan Bowen’s only attempt to get a credit card came during her first year at university. The bank rejected her because she had no income, reinforcing her belief that cards were meant for “people with stable incomes.”

Then, at 22, she found herself in debt anyway.

Last October, she realized she owed around 3,000 yuan ($400) — more than her entire monthly student allowance. With the debt weighing on her, she cut daily expenses, took on part-time work, and borrowed from friends to pay it down.

The debt had built up through apps she used every day to order takeout, buy groceries, and shop online, each offering the option to pay later or split purchases into installments.

Even so, Yan sees the relatively low limits on app-based credit as a safeguard against getting in too deep. “It keeps the risk manageable, nothing big enough to shock my parents,” she said. “A credit card would just mean higher risk.”

That wariness extends well beyond Yan. By the end of March 2026, China had about 687 million credit and combo cards in circulation, down roughly 120 million from their 2022 peak, according to central bank data.

Yan is one of 12 people aged 20 to 26, including students, job seekers, and office workers, whom Sixth Tone interviewed in July. Of them, nine had never owned a credit card. Many knew little about how cards worked and worried most about missing repayments. The few who did use cards tended to do so for specific reasons, such as overseas travel or managing cash flow.

More than 60 credit card subcenters closed across China in 2025, according to state-run People’s Daily, while some banks folded their card businesses and standalone apps into broader retail operations.

Yet outstanding balances on bank cards have remained relatively stable, said Jiang Jiajun, an associate professor at Fudan University’s School of Economics, in Shanghai. That suggests many of the cards being canceled were dormant rather than evidence that consumers had stopped borrowing. Even so, he said, “at least from the data, there is a clear trend of people avoiding credit cards.”

The traditional selling points — higher limits, longer interest-free periods, and richer rewards — may simply matter less to younger consumers. Those perks “are not necessarily what Gen Z cares most about,” Jiang said.

Yan’s first encounter with borrowing came through a food-delivery coupon. During her sophomore year, Chinese delivery app Meituan offered her a discount worth less than 1 yuan, but only if she activated its pay-later service. She did.

Before long, she had signed up for Huabei, a credit service inside Ant Group’s Alipay payment app, and Baitiao, a similar product from e-commerce giant JD.com. “They’re just so easy,” Yan said. “Even when traveling, hotels let you stay first and pay later.”

Even with enough money in the bank, Yan sometimes chose to pay later or in installments rather than watch her balance fall. Small debts piled up across different apps, and she often did not know the total until the monthly bill came due.

Her biggest current debt comes from a 6,500-yuan laptop. To be eligible for a student discount, Yan had to pay through Baitiao, so she split the cost into six monthly installments of more than 1,000 yuan. As of Aug. 5, she still owed more than 5,600 yuan.

Unlike credit cards, which require a separate application, app-based credit is built directly into services young consumers already use, often with lower limits and fewer steps between browsing and borrowing.

Jiang said the difference comes down partly to “mental accounting” — the way people sort spending into different mental buckets. Small, frequent purchases through apps like Huabei can feel like part of a “convenient lifestyle” rather than “financial debt.” Credit cards, by contrast, make the borrowing harder to ignore.

“They make users acutely aware that they are borrowing money, which naturally triggers resistance,” Jiang said. “These two things sit in completely different mental accounts for young people.”

For some young consumers, credit cards begin to look more useful as purchases get bigger and finances more secure.

Wang Xuanren, 23, works in finance in the eastern city of Nanjing and applied for her first and only credit card in 2024 ahead of an overseas trip. She already had more than 500,000 yuan in a fixed-term deposit at the bank, helping her secure approval the same day; the card arrived five days later.

She now saves it largely for electronics and luxury goods. For big-ticket purchases, Wang said installments can turn a 40,000- or 50,000-yuan expense into much smaller monthly payments, automatically deducted from her debit account.

“I keep a lot of cash on hand,” she said. “Using a credit card interest-free is basically borrowing someone else’s money and paying it back later.”

Zheng Yuxin, a 21-year-old university student in Shanghai, is far less comfortable with that bargain. She has no plans to apply for a credit card or use app-based credit anytime soon. “Nothing in life is free,” she said.

Even generous sign-up bonuses make her wary. Credit cards feel “very distant and risky,” she said. “I worry about falling for a scam because I can’t tell what’s real.”

In 2023, Zheng activated Huabei after agreeing to an authorization screen and completing facial verification. It then became her default payment method, allowing later purchases to be charged through the service without her actively choosing it each time.

She realized what had happened only when roughly 100 yuan was deducted from her bank account on repayment day. “Seeing unexpected money disappear gave me this empty, unsettled feeling,” she said. Since then, she has stuck to a simpler rule: buy only when she already has the money.

From Sept. 30, China will require a clearer separation between paying and borrowing online. Non-bank payment providers will no longer be allowed to present loans as payment options or market lending products through their payment services, with companies required to adjust their practices before the rules take effect.

Jiang said such rules should make borrowing more transparent and give users clearer warnings before they take on debt. The goal, he said, is not to eliminate app-based credit, but to make sure consumers know when an ordinary purchase has become a loan. “This protects consumers and helps platforms earn long-term trust,” he said.

Those preferences may change with age. Higher incomes, more travel, and larger spending needs could eventually make the higher limits and longer interest-free periods of credit cards more useful. “The same group of people might develop completely different habits 10 years from now,” said Jiang.

Zhang Xinyun, 24 and from the northeastern city of Harbin, is currently unemployed and remains deeply wary of credit cards after watching a relative struggle with card debt when she was a teenager. “Spending ahead always comes with bad temptations,” she said. High limits look more like added risk than freedom, and sign-up gifts do little to reassure her.

But Zhang can imagine her needs changing. Once she starts working or running a business, she said, a card could become useful for managing cash flow or traveling overseas.

Jiang underscores that banks cannot rely on that change happening on its own. “They need to improve convenience, embrace fintech, and create use cases that resonate with younger consumers.”

At the bank where Zhao Wei works in the northeastern city of Shenyang, signing up new credit card users is part of the job. She is expected to bring in dozens each year and, last year, even opened her own first card partly to help meet the target.

Many customers worry about missing repayments and damaging their credit records, Zhao said. Others simply see little need for a card when mobile payments and app-based credit are already woven into daily spending through digital services such as WeChat Pay, Alipay, and Huabei.

Banks have responded with incentives. Zhao’s gives new cardholders 150 yuan in spending credits, along with gifts ranging from rice and cooking oil to household appliances. Elsewhere, welcome offers can include health checkups, airport lounge access, fuel vouchers, coffee coupons, and cash back on purchases.

Zhao is blunt about how far such incentives can go. “People who are put off by credit cards won’t open one just for that,” she said.

More recently, her bank began offering customized cards printed with customers’ pet photos, along with discounts on pet supplies.

Even that has not made Zhao optimistic. “Credit cards are being squeezed by more convenient products,” she said. “If they can’t build stronger ties to daily life, becoming obsolete is not impossible.”

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: VCG)

World.title: Lost, Looted, Crumbling: The Vanishing Temple Murals of Yu County
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018887/Lost, Looted, Crumbling: The Vanishing Temple Murals of Yu County
World.content:
A Chinese county known as the home of over 400 temple murals dating back to the Ming dynasty (1368–1644) is facing a heritage restoration crisis, with many of its murals stolen, destroyed, or marred by thieves.

In an investigation published Wednesday, Shanghai-based news outlet The Paper visited 16 fortified villages in Yu County in the northern Hebei province and found that many of the area’s temple murals had been stolen, destroyed during temple collapse, or weathered beyond recognition. Remaining fragments often bore looters’ cut marks.

A major cultural relic hub, the county served as a military and commercial crossroads during the Ming and Qing dynasties (1644–1911) and is home to more than 1,600 registered cultural heritage locations, including numerous fortified villages. The accompanying temples feature murals depicting Taoist, Buddhist, and folk religious elements.

Danhou Village — inscribed on China’s official list of traditional villages in 2016 — is one of the county’s most popular tourist destinations. The village’s Guandi Temple was once home to extensive murals, but only fragments remain today.

When The Paper visited, the temple was under renovation for leaking roofs, missing wooden components, and cracked walls after years of neglect. Work began in April and is projected to be completed by the end of the year.

Of the 16 villages The Paper visited, only those officially considered “traditional villages” or protected sites received restoration and care. The report noted that overall neglect of the fortified villages stems from their abandonment, as villagers have mostly lived outside the sites since the 1980s, leaving the buildings to decay.

A member of the county’s cultural relics management office told The Paper that he recently inspected a temple on a visit to his hometown.

“I went there around noon, and the wall was still standing,” he said. “But at around 2 p.m., I got a call saying the western wall of that temple had collapsed. If I had gone any later, I might have been buried under it.”

Another obstacle to upkeep is funding. Under China’s cultural relics law, their owners or users must preserve them, with government subsidies provided where possible. But in Yu County, most low-level relics are owned by villages that can’t afford maintenance, placing the burden on the county.

The cultural relics worker described how every village has an appointed relic steward, but with no subsidy budget, the role falls to village cadres as an additional duty. With heavy workloads and no stipends, protection relies on individual goodwill.

Yet government investment has been considerable. Over a decade ago, Yu County built a 12,000-square-meter museum for 10,000-plus movable relics, free to the public, costing the county nearly 4 million yuan ($600,000) annually. In 2023, state and provincial funds for restoration projects totaled 14.6 million yuan.

Despite the investment, Yu County’s neglected relics expose gaps in China’s heritage architecture protection, a problem that it has been working to solve in recent years.

In July 2024, the Finance Ministry created a lottery-funded program for unlisted ancient buildings. Upon submitting a proposal, local authorities whose heritage architecture and restoration projects are deemed to serve the public good are given priority. The program will run through 2027.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Murals at an ancient temple in Yu County, Hebei province, June 20, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018886/The Forgotten Legacy of China’s Greatest Explorer
World.title: The Forgotten Legacy of China’s Greatest Explorer
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018886/The Forgotten Legacy of China’s Greatest Explorer
World.content:
During the opening decades of the 15th century, a eunuch from China’s imperial court led seven epic voyages across Southeast Asia and the Indian Ocean, pushing westward as far as the Red Sea and the shores of East Africa.

The expeditions were astonishing feats of engineering and navigation. Setting sail decades before Christopher Columbus or Vasco da Gama, Zheng He spent years crossing the oceans at the head of a vast fleet of 200 ships. Some of the vessels measured up to 70 meters long — three times the size of Columbus’ ships.

For many, Zheng deserves to rank among history’s greatest explorers. Yet, much about the voyages — and Zheng himself — remains shrouded in mystery. He barely features in the official records left by China’s Ming dynasty (1368–1644), with court historians dismissing his expeditions as impressive, but ruinously expensive. Even the place and date of Zheng’s death are unknown.

The Ming court’s assessment still colors views of Zheng centuries later. Today, the great admiral is well known in China, with generations of schoolchildren learning about his amazing treasure ships that brought giraffes, lions, zebras, and other exotic beasts back from Africa. But the voyages tend to be presented as a historical curiosity that had little lasting impact.

Zou Zhenhuan is on a mission to change that. The 69-year-old — now a distinguished professor at Shanghai’s Fudan University — has spent decades studying Zheng He, and his research has played a significant role in shifting perceptions of the explorer and his legacy. His latest book, “Monsoon Asia and Africa: Cultural Exchange and Zheng He’s Voyages,” is his most comprehensive look at the subject yet.

For Zou, Zheng’s voyages were far more influential than often assumed. Far from a flash in the pan, they opened up a new era of maritime trade between Asia and Africa, as merchants took advantage of the navigational technologies and sea routes pioneered by Zheng. He even believes they helped pave the way for the European Age of Discovery that followed.

In this interview, Zou, who is also a research fellow at the Shanghai Research Institute of Culture and History, explains why Zheng He is often so misunderstood — and why his voyages should be seen as a harbinger of globalization. The text has been edited for brevity and clarity.

Sixth Tone: You have studied Zheng He for more than 20 years. What drew you to this subject in the beginning?

Zou: My interest in Zheng He began in my boyhood. What captivated me most was his extraordinary perseverance — seven voyages spanning more than two decades. Such marvelous experiences are enough to stir the imagination. As the Portuguese poet Luís de Camões wrote in “Os Lusíadas,” the true and marvelous deeds of brave men surpass all fantasy and legend. I was a sickly boy, but I harbored an intense hero complex, and Zheng He’s exploits answered it perfectly.

It was this interest that led me to study Zheng He once I became a historian, and it is this same interest that has sustained my research for so many years.

Sixth Tone: After all these years of research, what kind of person is Zheng He in your mind?

Zou: As my research has deepened, the image of Zheng He in my mind has grown ever richer. Take his religious faith, for example. Many people might assume Zheng He was simply a Muslim. He was indeed born into a Muslim family; his grandfather and father both made the hajj to Mecca. But he was also a devout Buddhist who was accepted as a disciple by an eminent monk, receiving the Dharma name “Fushan,” and supervising the construction of the Great Bao’en Temple in Nanjing. At the same time, Zheng He was also an adherent of Confucianism. Historical records describe him as “endowed with the talent to govern and versed in the teachings of Confucius and Mencius.”

The most famous material testimony to Zheng He’s plural faith is the trilingual stele he erected in the kingdom of Ceylon (present-day Sri Lanka) during his second voyage in 1409. The stele, commonly known as the Galle Trilingual Inscription, is carved in three scripts: the Chinese text praises the Buddha and records a list of offerings; the Tamil text glorifies the Hindu god Shiva; and the Persian text extols Allah. Paying tribute to the deities of three great religions on a single stone tablet is, in my view, the most vivid expression of Zheng He’s cosmopolitan, all-embracing spirit.

Sixth Tone: It seems “plurality” is a keyword when it comes to Zheng He.

Zou: Exactly. Zheng He was a man of all-around talent. To begin with, he possessed exceptional organizational and managerial abilities — commanding a fleet of more than 27,000 men was in itself an enormously complex feat of systems engineering.

He also had the metaphysical learning of a Confucian scholar and was equally adept at practical, technical matters: during the voyages he spread the Chinese calendar, rituals, weights and measures, and architectural techniques to other countries, and with superb diplomatic skill he mediated disputes between Siam and Malacca, and between Annam and Champa.

Plus, he even displayed outstanding military talent: on his very first voyage he defeated Chen Zuyi, a pirate chief who commanded tens of thousands of followers in the Strait of Malacca, wiping out more than 5,000 pirates.

Sixth Tone: When I was reading your book, what impressed me most was Zheng He’s nautical technology — especially his precise understanding and ingenious use of the Indian Ocean monsoons.

Zou: That’s right. The fleet’s seven expeditions were deeply embedded in the monsoon, which is the main reason I titled the book “Monsoon Asia and Africa.”

The regions the fleet traversed — East Asia, Southeast Asia, and the Indian Ocean — are among the areas of the world where the monsoon phenomenon is most pronounced. And in an era without modern propulsion, the monsoon was the “engine” that drove this enormous armada on its long voyages.

The fleet usually departed China in winter, between October and March, riding the northeast monsoon southward. By the time it reached the Indian Ocean, the summer southwest monsoon would be blowing, allowing a smooth voyage home. The whole round trip took about a year and a half.

To visit more places efficiently, Zheng He would dispatch detached squadrons along the way; after completing their missions, these squadrons would regroup at designated rendezvous points in accordance with the monsoon patterns.

But here’s the thing: the monsoon and the compass could carry the fleet forward, but they could not tell the crew exactly where they were on the open sea. To do this, the fleet mastered a refined technique known as “guoyang qianxing,” or star-observation navigation, using an instrument called the “qianxing,” or star-measuring, board to determine a ship’s latitude according to stars’ altitude above the horizon. Zheng He’s fleets also compiled these observations into dedicated star charts, creating a reusable navigational database.

One could say that Zheng He’s fleet fused three techniques — the monsoon patterns, star-observation navigation, and the magnetic compass — into a single, world-leading navigational system for its time. I believe these sea routes, nautical technology, and geographical knowledge helped lay the intellectual and technical foundations for the arrival of European explorers more than half a century later. However, this topic needs further research.

Sixth Tone: Since you mention the European explorers who came later, I have to raise a common critique: that unlike the explorers who launched Europe’s Age of Discovery, Zheng He’s expeditions — for all their grandeur — were a mere flash in the pan that left no lasting imprint. How do you see it?

Zou: This view is indeed very common. I would point out that Zheng He’s seven voyages were not merely official acts of diplomacy by the Ming court; they also facilitated exchanges of goods, species, and technologies between Asia and Africa on an unprecedented scale.

The exotic animals the fleet brought back from foreign lands — giraffes, lions, ostriches, zebras — and the rare plants and fruits such as pepper, sappanwood, and durian greatly enriched China’s native stock of species. Wherever it went, the fleet shared nautical and astronomical knowledge with local peoples, deepening mutual learning among the civilizations of Asia and Africa.

The most representative example of all this is blue-and-white porcelain. Zheng He’s fleet carried large quantities of porcelain into the Islamic world, while the cobalt pigment needed to produce blue-and-white ware, known as “Sumali blue,” originally came from Persia. This pattern of “bringing finished products out and importing raw materials in” was itself a cross-cultural dialogue of technology and aesthetics.

As the Ming dynasty’s most sought-after export in overseas markets, blue-and-white porcelain was among the important gifts carried on every mission. Pieces dating from the period of Zheng He’s voyages have been unearthed at Fustat in Egypt, at Aydhab in Sudan, at Aden on the Arabian Peninsula, and elsewhere.

The huge overseas demand, in turn, stimulated a massive increase in early Ming porcelain production: according to historical records, in 1433 alone the court ordered the firing of 443,500 pieces in a single decree.

What does this tell us? It shows that nearly a century before Columbus set sail, Zheng He’s fleet had already opened up the east-west sea routes of the Indian Ocean and built a regional network of trade and cultural exchange. I call this the “Zheng He exchange.”

Sixth Tone: That concept readily brings to mind the “Columbian exchange” — the massive exchange of people, plants, animals, and diseases between the Americas and Afro-Eurasia that opened up after Columbus’ voyages.

Zou: I did indeed borrow the theoretical framework of the “Columbian exchange,” but my concept points to an earlier wave of civilizational interaction — one that unfolded between Asia and Africa. In many respects, Zheng He was a key catalyst on the eve of globalization.

Of course, while the “Zheng He exchange” and the “Columbian exchange” share many similarities, their purposes were fundamentally different. Zheng He’s voyages never established colonies overseas, and they were extremely restrained in their use of force.

As you mentioned, many Chinese people feel rather regretful about this, believing it caused China to miss a golden opportunity to dominate the globe. Liu Cixin’s short science-fiction story “Xiyang” (“The Western Ocean”) expresses exactly this sentiment through an alternate-history framework: in the story, Zheng He’s fleet sails farther west from the East African coast, rounds the Cape of Good Hope, and eventually reaches Europe, defeats the combined Anglo-French forces, and conquers the European continent, turning China into an empire on which the sun never sets.

But in my view, Zheng He radiates the light of pacifism and cultural pluralism — and that is precisely where his example can offer inspiration for our own time.

(Header image: A statue of Zheng He in Hangzhou, Zhejiang province, 2024. 500px Essential)

World.title: Tropical Depression Neneng intensifies; enhanced southwest monsoon brings more rain
World.content:
FORECAST. PAGASA Weather Specialist Chenel Dominguez explains the bureau's 5 am forecast for Tropical Depression Neneng inside the Philippine Area of Responsibility, and the two tropical depressions outside PAR, on August 19, 2026.

There are no rainfall warnings or tropical cyclone wind signals raised due to Tropical Depression Neneng, but warnings because of the southwest monsoon are still in effect on Wednesday, August 19

MANILA, Philippines – Tropical Depression Neneng slightly intensified before dawn on Wednesday, August 19, while enhancing the southwest monsoon or habagat, which remains the country’s major source of rain.

Neneng’s maximum sustained winds increased from 45 kilometers per hour to 55 km/h, said the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) in a briefing past 5 am on Wednesday. The tropical depression’s gustiness is now up to 70 km/h from 55 km/h.

As of 4 am, Neneng was already 675 kilometers east of Itbayat, Batanes, moving northwest at 15 km/h.

The tropical depression is unlikely to make landfall in the Philippines. Instead, it could make landfall in Taiwan between Thursday afternoon, August 20, and Friday morning, August 21. Taiwan is within the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR).

PAGASA also said Neneng may weaken into a remnant low over or near Taiwan by Friday morning.

There are no rainfall warnings or tropical cyclone wind signals raised due to Neneng, but warnings because of the southwest monsoon are still in effect.

PAGASA’s updated rainfall outlook for the southwest monsoon, released at 5 am on Wednesday, covers the next 48 hours. Wednesday remains critical for Metro Manila and 17 provinces, while most of these areas might begin to see gradually improving weather on Thursday. Floods and landslides can still occur.

Wednesday, August 19

Heavy to intense rain (100-200 millimeters): Zambales, Bataan, Occidental Mindoro

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Metro Manila, La Union, Benguet, Pangasinan, Ilocos Sur, Abra, Tarlac, Pampanga, Bulacan, Nueva Ecija, Cavite, Batangas, Laguna, Rizal, Oriental Mindoro

Thursday, August 20

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, La Union, Pangasinan, Zambales, Bataan

For Wednesday, the rest of Luzon as well as Antique and Aklan may also have scattered rain and thunderstorms due to the southwest monsoon.

PAGASA added that the southwest monsoon is bringing strong to gale-force gusts to these areas:

Wednesday, August 19, and Thursday, August 20

most of Luzon, most of Visayas, Zamboanga Peninsula, Northern Mindanao, Davao Region

Friday, August 21

most of Luzon, Panay Island, Negros Occidental, Northern Samar, Davao Oriental

Moderate to rough sea conditions will persist on Wednesday, too.

Up to rough seas (small vessels should not venture out to sea)

Seaboards of Zambales and Lubang Islands; western seaboards of Babuyan Islands, Bataan, and Pangasinan; northern seaboard of Ilocos Norte – waves up to 3.5 meters high

Seaboards of Ilocos Sur and La Union; remaining seaboards of Babuyan Islands, Ilocos Norte, and Pangasinan; western seaboards of Batangas and Occidental Mindoro; northern and western seaboards of Calamian Islands and Kalayaan Islands; southern seaboard of Bataan – waves up to 3 meters high

Up to moderate seas (small vessels should take precautionary measures or avoid sailing, if possible)

Seaboard of Surigao del Sur; western seaboards of Cavite and northern mainland Palawan; eastern seaboard of Davao Oriental; remaining seaboards of Occidental Mindoro and Kalayaan Islands – waves up to 2.5 meters high

Seaboards of Isabela, northern Aurora, Romblon, Cuyo Islands, Cagayancillo Islands, Antique, and Davao Occidental; northern and eastern seaboards of Catanduanes; eastern seaboards of Dinagat Islands and Siargao-Bucas Grande Islands; southern seaboards of Oriental Mindoro, Marinduque, Quezon, and Iloilo; remaining seaboards of Palawan and Davao Oriental – waves up to 2 meters high

Neneng is the Philippines’ 14th tropical cyclone for 2026, and the third tropical cyclone for August, after Tropical Depression Luis and Tropical Storm Maymay (Kujira).

Aside from Neneng, there are now two tropical depressions being monitored outside PAR.

The low pressure area that PAGASA has been monitoring over the West Philippine Sea developed into a tropical depression at 8 pm on Tuesday, August 20.

As of 3 am on Wednesday, this tropical depression was located 670 kilometers west of Calayan, Cagayan, moving west at 20 km/h. It has maximum sustained winds of 45 km/h and gustiness of up to 55 km/h.

The tropical depression is not expected to enter PAR, as it is heading for China. However, it may help enhance the southwest monsoon.

Meanwhile, the other tropical depression outside PAR was last spotted 3,090 kilometers east of northeastern Mindanao, slowly moving west at 3 am on Wednesday. Its maximum sustained winds increased from 45 km/h to 55 km/h, while its gustiness is now up to 70 km/h from 55 km/h.

PAGASA Weather Specialist Chenel Dominguez said there is still high uncertainty in the forecast for this tropical cyclone given its distance from the Philippines, but it might also enhance the southwest monsoon in the last week of August.

The weather bureau estimated that up to four tropical cyclones may develop within or enter PAR during the month. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Vantage Point] What is ABS-CBN’s stock-market listing still worth?
World.content:
The burden of proving the economic usefulness of ABS-CBN's listing on the Philippine Stock Exchange has changed

ABS-CBN’s P6-billion recapitalization would leave its public float dramatically smaller even as private investors supply the capital the company urgently needs. That does not mean delisting is imminent, but it raises a harder question: if ownership, financing and control are becoming increasingly concentrated outside the public market, what exactly is ABS-CBN’s stock-market listing still worth?

ABS-CBN’s P6-billion recapitalization has forced me to look beyond the question of who is putting money into the company.

There is another question hiding in plain sight: after the transaction is completed, what exactly will ABS-CBN still gain from remaining listed on the Philippine Stock Exchange (PSE)?

I am not suggesting that ABS-CBN plans to delist. There is no disclosure saying that.

One factual distinction is important. ABS-CBN’s latest Public Ownership Report, dated June 30, still shows 899.85 million common shares outstanding and 374.55 million shares in public hands, equivalent to a 41.62% public float.

The roughly 15% figure we have been discussing is therefore not the company’s present reported float. It is the estimated result if the proposed issuance of more than 1.64 billion new common shares to I&C Holdings and Lopez-related investors is completed without a corresponding increase in publicly held shares.

The transaction would dramatically expand ABS-CBN’s common-share base while leaving the number of shares held by existing public investors essentially unchanged. On that assumption, the public would fall from more than two-fifths of the common equity to roughly one-seventh.

ABS-CBN would remain above the 10% minimum public-ownership requirement applicable to a company listed as long ago as 1992. So, this is not yet a forced-delisting story.

It is an economic one.

The Philippine market has seen variations of this progression before. Energy Development Corp. (EDC) eventually went private after strategic investors accumulated overwhelming ownership and its owners decided that greater flexibility over capital allocation and long-term decisions outweighed the benefits of remaining public.

Metro Pacific Investments Corp. showed another route. Its controlling shareholders concluded that the market persistently undervalued the infrastructure group relative to the underlying worth of its assets. They eventually bought out minorities and delisted the company.

Keppel Philippines Holdings and 8990 Holdings demonstrated how concentrated ownership, weak liquidity, and frustration over market valuation can progressively diminish the usefulness of a public listing. Holcim Philippines and Pepsi-Cola Products Philippines showed the regulatory endgame once public ownership falls beneath the required minimum.

ABS-CBN is nowhere near that stage. That needs to be said plainly.

But the latest filings beg for answers because this is not simply a company concentrating ownership while generating abundant cash.

ABS-CBN ended 2025 with only P747 million in consolidated stockholders’ equity, down from P2.52 billion a year earlier. Current liabilities stood at P22.56 billion against current assets of only P10.12 billion.

By March 31, consolidated equity had slipped slightly negative, while current liabilities had risen to P23.32 billion against P9.85 billion of current assets. The company lost P813 million in the first quarter alone. (READ: ABS-CBN is now 84% content — and still losing money. Can P6 billion fix it?)

That changes the meaning of the P6-billion infusion.

This is not merely growth capital entering a healthy listed company. It is capital arriving when ABS-CBN’s balance sheet badly needs reinforcement.

And crucially, that capital is not being raised from the public market.

The PSE’s June ownership report shows Lopez Inc. holding 502.26 million common shares, or 55.82%, before the recapitalization, while public investors held 374.55 million. Yet the new money is coming principally from I&C Holdings and Lopez-related private vehicles rather than through a rights offering or broad public issuance.

That is where the conventional rationale for being listed begins to turn upside down.

A stock exchange is supposed to connect companies requiring capital with investors willing to provide it. Listing provides access to equity financing, liquidity, price discovery, and acquisition currency. It also imposes costs: disclosures, governance requirements, shareholder meetings, listing fees, and scrutiny from minority investors.

For ABS-CBN, those obligations may still be worthwhile. There are particularly strong arguments for a media institution remaining public. Public-company status subjects it to continuing disclosure obligations and gives ordinary investors participation in one of the country’s most recognizable media brands. Its shares could someday again become useful financing or acquisition currency.

But the recapitalization weakens one traditional justification.

ABS-CBN is obtaining the principal economic benefit of an equity market—new permanent capital—without obtaining that capital from the investing public.

There is another irony. Before the new shares are issued, ABS-CBN has fewer than 900 million common shares outstanding and a public float above 40%. After the contemplated recapitalization, it could have roughly 2.54 billion common shares outstanding while the public’s absolute shareholdings barely change.

The company would become far larger in share count but much smaller in public participation.

That does not mean delisting follows. Nor does concentrated common ownership necessarily mean the Lopez family loses voting control, because ABS-CBN’s voting preferred shares must be considered separately from common economic ownership.

It means something narrower.

The burden of proving the economic usefulness of the listing begins to change.

For decades, asking why ABS-CBN should remain listed would have seemed almost absurd. The answers were obvious: capital, liquidity, valuation, visibility, and broad public ownership.

After this recapitalization, I find myself asking the question in reverse.

If private investors can provide billions of pesos when the company most desperately needs capital, if public shareholders fall from 41.62% of the common equity to roughly 15%, and if trading liquidity subsequently contracts as ownership concentrates, what exactly is the stock-market listing still worth?

The Philippine precedents do not tell us that ABS-CBN will leave the PSE.

They tell us the circumstances under which listed companies eventually begin asking themselves the same question. – Rappler.com

World.title: LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte
World.content:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.

On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.
