World.title: Suaalii positional shift flagged in Wallabies squad for Argentina
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Suaalii positional shift flagged in Wallabies squad for Argentina Iain Payten August 19, 2026 — 11:32am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Coach Les Kiss has flagged a potential move for Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii into the Wallabies’ back three after the NSW superstar was cleared to return from a hamstring injury for the two-Test tour of Argentina. Kiss released a largely unchanged Wallabies squad on Wednesday for the series with the Pumas, which will see them clash in San Salvador de Jujuy on August 30 and Mendoza on September 6. Loading The two major additions from the Wallabies squads that downed Japan in Osaka and Townsville were Len Ikitau, who missed both games with an ankle injury, and Suaalii, who was out from the big win at the weekend in Townsville with a hamstring problem. In an interesting twist, however, one of the men who dropped out the squad to make room for the star duo was fullback Jock Campbell, just a few days after the 31-year-old was named as Queensland’s best player.



Campbell started for the Wallabies in the first Test of the year against Ireland before being contentiously moved to the bench for the Test against France in Brisbane, where he was used as a five-eighth. Campbell has since not featured for the Wallabies. After coming in for Suaalii in Townsville, Josh Flook also dropped out of the squad, but Kiss has not made room for Ikitau and Suaalii by dropping any other of his centres; namely Hunter Paisami and Isaac Henry. Len Ikitau and Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii celebrate after Max Jorgensen’s winning try in 2024. AP Both turned in outstanding performances for the Wallabies as a starting midfield in Townsville, with Henry playing strongly at No.13 in his run-on debut. His form prompted questions post-game about whether Suaalii might be looked at as a winger or fullback. The omission of Campbell suggests Kiss may be considering that for the Argentina trip.



Kiss moved Suaalii to wing in Osaka when Henry entered the game in the second half. Tom Wright is the starting fullback, but with Campbell gone, the back-up would be between Max Jorgensen, Suaalii and Ben Donaldson. In other news, Tom Hooper has also been named in the squad, and as forecast, Taniela Tupou will also tour Argentina. The pair play for overseas clubs but are remaining with the Wallabies under World Rugby’s regulation 9. The rule allows the mandatory release of players by clubs for Test rugby. With one more game of a suspension to serve, Miles Amatosero was also left out.



Kiss said in statement: “As coaches we’ve looked to maintain consistency in selection with the bulk of this squad having laid a solid foundation over the past few weeks, through their hard work and connection on and off the field. “Touring Argentina presents another tough challenge for us as a new group, and it’s one that we know will require us to go to another level as we continue to look to build and develop our game.”

World.title: ‘He’s never liked her’: Palmer backs Nationals to take on Hanson and Rinehart
World.content:
Breaking PoliticsFederalOne Nation ‘He’s never liked her’: Palmer backs Nationals to take on Hanson and Rinehart Paul Sakkal August 19, 2026 — 11:32am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Nationals are hopeful that billionaire Clive Palmer’s alleged dislike of Pauline Hanson will encourage him to pump millions into Coalition coffers to fend off the insurgency threatening to wipe out the country party. Palmer, as first reported by this masthead on Monday, was a surprise guest at the party’s annual dinner in Canberra on Saturday where he spent about $25,000 in an auction to purchase country music star Lee Kernaghan’s guitar. Billionaire Clive Palmer pictured sharing a birthday cake with One Nation leader Pauline Hanson in May. x.com/PaulineHansonOz Sources in the party claimed the mining magnate and perennial political activist had started donating hundreds of thousands in addition to the auction purchase, but the party did not confirm this figure and Palmer’s staff did not return calls. “From what I’ve heard, he has never liked her, full-stop,” Nationals president Andrew Fraser said of Palmer’s views of Hanson.



Coalition figures were surprised when Palmer was photographed meeting Hanson on May 27 when he brought a cake for the senator’s birthday. Two days earlier, Palmer registered “United Nation” with IP Australia, an apparent amalgam of United Australia Party and One Nation. In 2024, before Hanson’s popularity took off, Palmer offered $10 million to create a tie-up with One Nation. The deal went nowhere partly because Hanson demanded she be president for life. Nationals in Canberra held the same view as Fraser and believed that Palmer was motivated by putting a roadblock on Hanson’s path to The Lodge. “He’s not a fan and doesn’t believe in the hype,” one senior Nationals MPs said. Senator Matthew Canavan gets along well with Clive Palmer Dominic Lorrimer Palmer’s latest moves have buoyed new Nationals leader Matt Canavan and sets up a battle between Hanson, who is backed by Australia’s richest woman Gina Rinehart, and the Coalition, which hopes Palmer might put big money behind the ailing centre-right party before donations are limited by new laws starting next year.



“It would be nice if we could utilise him or his resources at the next election because things are pretty tight,” Fraser said, adding that Palmer, a long-time Nationals figure, had “come home”. The Nationals were starved of funds under former leader David Littleproud, who did not attract conservative donors. One Nation’s surge has made life even more difficult for the Liberal and National parties, who are on track to lose a swag of seats to One Nation. Nationals defector Barnaby Joyce, a strong fundraiser, and Pauline Hanson have been hosting intimate dinners with wealthy Australians on Rinehart’s private jet, at Rinehart’s home, and at other locations such as Dubbo, NSW, where Joyce held a fundraiser at the weekend. The Palmer move is key because a January 1, 2027 deadline for large donations is just over four months away. The government passed laws capping at $50,000 per year the amount any one donor can give to a party per year. The laws were designed in large part to prohibit a repeat of Palmer’s 2019 effort where he donated tens of millions to his United Australia Party to stop Bill Shorten being elected.



Despite millions being spent since 2019 on his famous yellow-coloured ads, Palmer has failed to turn the UAP into an influential political force. It only has one elected official: the Victorian senator Ralph Babet. Fraser said he expected Hanson and Nationals defector Joyce would feud and that voters would shift away from Hanson over time as they realised she ran a “protest party”, not one that could govern. Contrasting One Nation with the organic debate that occurred at the Nationals conference on the weekend, Fraser said: “Pauline’s party is not a party: it’s an autocratic organisation where she pulls all the strings.” “They have not fixed a piece of road oe built one bridge, nothing. They’re a protest party and at the end of the day I think people will see through that.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. One Nation’s Queensland division has filed three years of overdue financial returns after the regulator threatened to strip the party of its legal status in its home state.

World.title: Australia news LIVE: Gambling reform package passes House of Representatives; MPs ‘deeply disturbed’ by responses to Swans, Scots allegations as they take aim at institutions
World.content:
NSW Labor Premier Chris Minns has called for the tobacco excise to be slashed after Pauline Hanson said this week she would cut the tax by 75 per cent.

“I’ve been calling for the same thing for about a year,” Minns said on ABC TV this morning. “So it’d be pretty disingenuous to come on after One Nation agreed with that policy and say they’re wrong.”

Minns said the excise was not working as intended and was “really a source of funding and opportunity for organised crime”.

“The grim reality is that the excise has pushed up the legal cost of cigarettes in our economy and, at the same time, the black market has exploded. So, rather perversely, rather than the cost of cigarettes declining and less people smoking, we’re seeing accessibility and affordability plunge and, as a result, people are smoking, it seems to me, at massive numbers.”

He said NSW was pouring “enormous resources” into policing the underground tobacco trade, and warned the situation would only get worse with the excise due to rise again.

World.title: Ukraine’s ousted defence minister calls for wartime elections
World.content:
WorldEuropeRussia-Ukraine war Ukraine’s ousted defence minister calls for wartime elections Max Hunder Updated August 19, 2026 — 11:42am ,first published 10:49am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Kyiv: Ukraine’s recently ousted defence minister, Mykhailo Fedorov, has called for wartime elections in a bombshell address, arguing that the nation faces a crisis of governance, in the biggest internal challenge to President Volodymyr Zelensky since Russia’s invasion. Fedorov’s call, delivered in a video address posted on social media on Tuesday (Ukraine time), is the first such demand by a major Ukrainian political figure since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022. Ukrainian law prohibits holding elections during wartime. Mykhailo Fedorov in his office in 2023. The New York Times “Democracy cannot be held hostage by Russia,” Fedorov said. “We must find a legal, safe and realistic mechanism that will allow Ukraine to renew its full democratic process even in the conditions of a long war.” The 35-year-old Fedorov was a longtime ally of Zelensky’s until his unexpected firing from the Defence Ministry in July, just six months after he had been appointed, vowing sweeping reforms.



Shortly after his dismissal, the tech-savvy Fedorov publicly tore into the commander-in-chief of the armed forces, Oleksandr Syrskyi, exposing a bitter rift between the men and their different visions for the war. Related Article Analysis

Russia-Ukraine war Feud between Zelensky and his army chief is boiling over – and Russia loves it Thousands of Ukrainians took to the streets to demand the sacking of Syrskyi – an old-guard military commander blamed by his critics for heavy troop losses at the front line – and Fedorov’s reinstatement. Although Zelensky said he had dismissed Fedorov for his inability to work with Syrskyi, the president fired the military chief shortly afterwards amid public pressure. Protests in support of Fedorov have continued for the past month, losing some of their early momentum but still regularly drawing a couple of thousand attendees in Kyiv.



While Fedorov did not say in his address that he would contest any election, a recent poll indicated the ex-minister would comfortably beat Zelensky in a run-off vote, where the top two presidential candidates go head-to-head. Challenge to Zelensky Fedorov’s statement came just hours after Zelensky confirmed he had asked parliament to confirm new Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara in office on Wednesday. In what appeared to be an open challenge to Zelensky, Fedorov said Ukraine faced a “systemic crisis of governance”.



“The old system lives by its own rules too often. It protects itself. It is scared of change,” he said. Drone warfare has become increasingly integral to Ukraine’s strategy. AP Without naming names, Fedorov condemned official corruption, which he said was hurting Ukraine’s war effort. The ex-minister recently said he believed his reforms of the Defence Ministry’s procurement processes, which are responsible for purchasing billions of dollars’ worth of equipment, contributed to his sacking. Zelensky’s office had no immediate comment on Fedorov’s address.



Fedorov became Ukraine’s youngest-ever minister at 28 in 2019 when he was appointed digitalisation chief by the newly elected Zelensky. He was the last remaining member of Zelensky’s first cabinet. His role running the Ministry of Digital Transformation saw him become an early adopter of drone warfare, which has turned combat in Ukraine on its head since 2022. However, his nationwide profile grew significantly after his appointment to lead the vast Defence Ministry in January, when he immediately vowed a data-driven overhaul. Unlike his predecessors, Fedorov publicly laid out a strategy to defeat Russia through attrition and technological superiority. “Our people have long been ready for a different country,” Fedorov said in his address. “Now, our state must become worthy of its people.” Reuters Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Suaalii positional shift flagged in Wallabies squad for Argentina
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Suaalii positional shift flagged in Wallabies squad for Argentina Iain Payten August 19, 2026 — 11:32am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Coach Les Kiss has flagged a potential move for Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii into the Wallabies’ back three after the NSW superstar was cleared to return from a hamstring injury for the two-Test tour of Argentina. Kiss released a largely unchanged Wallabies squad on Wednesday for the series with the Pumas, which will see them clash in San Salvador de Jujuy on August 30 and Mendoza on September 6. Loading The two major additions from the Wallabies squads that downed Japan in Osaka and Townsville were Len Ikitau, who missed both games with an ankle injury, and Suaalii, who was out from the big win at the weekend in Townsville with a hamstring problem. In an interesting twist, however, one of the men who dropped out the squad to make room for the star duo was fullback Jock Campbell, just a few days after the 31-year-old was named as Queensland’s best player.



Campbell started for the Wallabies in the first Test of the year against Ireland before being contentiously moved to the bench for the Test against France in Brisbane, where he was used as a five-eighth. Campbell has since not featured for the Wallabies. After coming in for Suaalii in Townsville, Josh Flook also dropped out of the squad, but Kiss has not made room for Ikitau and Suaalii by dropping any other of his centres; namely Hunter Paisami and Isaac Henry. Len Ikitau and Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii celebrate after Max Jorgensen’s winning try in 2024. AP Both turned in outstanding performances for the Wallabies as a starting midfield in Townsville, with Henry playing strongly at No.13 in his run-on debut. His form prompted questions post-game about whether Suaalii might be looked at as a winger or fullback. The omission of Campbell suggests Kiss may be considering that for the Argentina trip.



Kiss moved Suaalii to wing in Osaka when Henry entered the game in the second half. Tom Wright is the starting fullback, but with Campbell gone, the back-up would be between Max Jorgensen, Suaalii and Ben Donaldson. In other news, Tom Hooper has also been named in the squad, and as forecast, Taniela Tupou will also tour Argentina. The pair play for overseas clubs but are remaining with the Wallabies under World Rugby’s regulation 9. The rule allows the mandatory release of players by clubs for Test rugby. With one more game of a suspension to serve, Miles Amatosero was also left out.



Kiss said in statement: “As coaches we’ve looked to maintain consistency in selection with the bulk of this squad having laid a solid foundation over the past few weeks, through their hard work and connection on and off the field. “Touring Argentina presents another tough challenge for us as a new group, and it’s one that we know will require us to go to another level as we continue to look to build and develop our game.”

World.title: ‘He’s never liked her’: Palmer backs Nationals to take on Hanson and Rinehart
World.content:
Breaking PoliticsFederalOne Nation ‘He’s never liked her’: Palmer backs Nationals to take on Hanson and Rinehart Paul Sakkal August 19, 2026 — 11:32am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Nationals are hopeful that billionaire Clive Palmer’s alleged dislike of Pauline Hanson will encourage him to pump millions into Coalition coffers to fend off the insurgency threatening to wipe out the country party. Palmer, as first reported by this masthead on Monday, was a surprise guest at the party’s annual dinner in Canberra on Saturday where he spent about $25,000 in an auction to purchase country music star Lee Kernaghan’s guitar. Billionaire Clive Palmer pictured sharing a birthday cake with One Nation leader Pauline Hanson in May. x.com/PaulineHansonOz Sources in the party claimed the mining magnate and perennial political activist had started donating hundreds of thousands in addition to the auction purchase, but the party did not confirm this figure and Palmer’s staff did not return calls. “From what I’ve heard, he has never liked her, full-stop,” Nationals president Andrew Fraser said of Palmer’s views of Hanson.



Coalition figures were surprised when Palmer was photographed meeting Hanson on May 27 when he brought a cake for the senator’s birthday. Two days earlier, Palmer registered “United Nation” with IP Australia, an apparent amalgam of United Australia Party and One Nation. In 2024, before Hanson’s popularity took off, Palmer offered $10 million to create a tie-up with One Nation. The deal went nowhere partly because Hanson demanded she be president for life. Nationals in Canberra held the same view as Fraser and believed that Palmer was motivated by putting a roadblock on Hanson’s path to The Lodge. “He’s not a fan and doesn’t believe in the hype,” one senior Nationals MPs said. Senator Matthew Canavan gets along well with Clive Palmer Dominic Lorrimer Palmer’s latest moves have buoyed new Nationals leader Matt Canavan and sets up a battle between Hanson, who is backed by Australia’s richest woman Gina Rinehart, and the Coalition, which hopes Palmer might put big money behind the ailing centre-right party before donations are limited by new laws starting next year.



“It would be nice if we could utilise him or his resources at the next election because things are pretty tight,” Fraser said, adding that Palmer, a long-time Nationals figure, had “come home”. The Nationals were starved of funds under former leader David Littleproud, who did not attract conservative donors. One Nation’s surge has made life even more difficult for the Liberal and National parties, who are on track to lose a swag of seats to One Nation. Nationals defector Barnaby Joyce, a strong fundraiser, and Pauline Hanson have been hosting intimate dinners with wealthy Australians on Rinehart’s private jet, at Rinehart’s home, and at other locations such as Dubbo, NSW, where Joyce held a fundraiser at the weekend. The Palmer move is key because a January 1, 2027 deadline for large donations is just over four months away. The government passed laws capping at $50,000 per year the amount any one donor can give to a party per year. The laws were designed in large part to prohibit a repeat of Palmer’s 2019 effort where he donated tens of millions to his United Australia Party to stop Bill Shorten being elected.



Despite millions being spent since 2019 on his famous yellow-coloured ads, Palmer has failed to turn the UAP into an influential political force. It only has one elected official: the Victorian senator Ralph Babet. Fraser said he expected Hanson and Nationals defector Joyce would feud and that voters would shift away from Hanson over time as they realised she ran a “protest party”, not one that could govern. Contrasting One Nation with the organic debate that occurred at the Nationals conference on the weekend, Fraser said: “Pauline’s party is not a party: it’s an autocratic organisation where she pulls all the strings.” “They have not fixed a piece of road oe built one bridge, nothing. They’re a protest party and at the end of the day I think people will see through that.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Te Papa chief executive Courtney Johnston announces resignation
World.content:
The chief executive of national museum Te Papa in Wellington has resigned after six-and-a-half years in the job.

Courtney Johnston led the museum through the difficulties of Covid lockdowns and celebrations like the official launch of the Matariki public holiday.

Johnston first worked at Te Papa as a visitor host nearly 25 years ago.

She became chief executive in 2019 after working in roles at City Gallery Wellington, the National Library of New Zealand, and as the director of The Dowse Art Museum and Petone Settlers Museum Te Whare Whaakaro o Pito-one between 2012 to 2018.

She was also chair of the umbrella group Museums Aotearoa and a regular visual arts commentator for RNZ's Nine to Noon from 2010 to 2019.

In a statement, Johnston said the position had been "a huge part of my life, personally and professionally".

Te Papa's unseen national art collection Nights Download MP3 17m

She cited work behind the scenes leading up to the repatriation of koiwi tangata on Te Papa's marae as well as public moments as the face of the museum as "incredibly rewarding" experiences in the role.

"I've been there as we've returned taonga to their people, on their marae. I've helped add a specimen to our botany collection. I stood at the front door when we closed the museum for the first Covid lockdown, and stood at the front door again when we welcomed visitors back in. I have so many indelible memories from this time," Johnston said.

She believed she would be leaving the museum in a stronger position than she found it.

"Being appointed Tumu Whakarae was a dream, and the role has offered me more than I could ever have imagined.

"Leading within Te Papa's unique co-leadership model has been a particular privilege, and I thank Kaihautū Arapata Hakiwai for all his support over my tenure."

Johnston first worked at Te Papa as a visitor host nearly 25 years ago. Neil Price / Te Papa

Dr Arapata Hakiwai said Johnston had been "deeply instrumental" in advancing Te Papa's bicultural kaupapa and commitment to the museum's mana taonga principle.

"She has been a strong and compassionate leader and shown deep care for the taonga we are responsible for and the communities we serve. She will be very much missed by both our kaimahi and the communities we work with," Hakiwai said.

Johnston said she was looking forward to "recharging" and exploring some creative projects before her next step.

Te Papa Board chair Chris Swasbrook said Johnston had led with "passion and determination" during her time at the museum.

"The museum has faced a number of significant challenges, including the Covid period, the closure of our specialist collection facility, and the pressures of the economic recession.

"With the first year of construction for our new Biodiversity Research Centre completed and a programme of financial strengthening well underway, she leaves the museum well positioned for its next period of growth," Swasbrook said.

World.title: Reviewer appointed to probe second Immigration IT project
World.content:
The Public Service Commission has appointed a reviewer into another Ministry of Business, Innovation, and Employment IT project, this time to look at its programme to modernise Immigration New Zealand's systems and services.

The Our Future Services (OFS) programme is a $336 million, seven-year plan to make visa processing more efficient, mitigate the risks of technology and service failures, provide proactive and sophisticated risk management, and improve customer and user experience.

Following the launch of a review into the Biometric Capability Update project, including whether officials misled ministers, Immigration Minister Erica Stanford asked the commission to look at the broader OFS programme.

Public Service Commissioner Sir Brian Roche said the assurance review would provide confidence on cost, governance, management, reporting, and delivery of expected benefits.

"It is important that significant public sector programmes are subject to appropriate scrutiny and assurance. This review will help provide that assurance," he said.

World.title: Police officer says riding horse to work 'ticked off bucket-list goal'
World.content:
A police officer who rode a horse named Kitty to work says they wanted to "tick off a bucket-list goal", and had no idea how much attention his unusual mode of transport would attract.

RNZ earlier reported that a police officer rode his horse into work at the Christchurch Central Police Station in April.

It's understood the horse caught the attention of fellow staff after it was stationed at the Christchurch Central Police Station alongside more conventional transport options, such as bicycles and scooters.

Christchurch metro area commander Superintendent Lane Todd earlier said the horse was "saddled up with the bicycles for about an hour".

"This is nay an approved vehicle that can be parked onsite, and the officer was told to hold his horses, he did not have free rein to keep the horse there. It has since been scratched and sent home."

The officer wrote about his trip to work in the latest Police News magazine saying they "wanted to clear some stuff up".

"My horse, Kitty, is a 15-year-old Hanoverian mare and my main working horse when I go mustering.

"Riding her into work was something I'd talked about for more than a year."

The officer said before riding the horse to work they made sure everyone who needed to know was aware of his plans, including the district commander and building management team.

"I even did a health and safety plan as per Police policy and went through relevant legislation and bylaws to make sure what I was doing was legal.

"We left before dawn and arrived in the city just before 6am. For me, riding a horse is nothing unusual. I had no idea how much attention it would attract."

The officer said a couple of hours into his shift "my phone was off the charts".

"Bosses told me I hadn't done anything wrong, but they didn't want media attention during pay round. I was asked to take Kitty home. I did so without argument and the ride back turned into a memorable experience in itself.

"What stood out for me was the reaction from the public and colleagues. People stopped to chat, ask questions and take photos. Lots of staff told me it brightened their day, and some even said it was a career highlight."

The officer said there was "never any ulterior motive or protest".

"I genuinely just wanted to tick off a bucket-list goal and hopefully bring a smile to a few faces.

"In the end, no wrongdoing was found, Kitty returned to living her life back in the hills and I was reminded how much goodwill there is towards police when people get to see us simply as fellow Kiwis."

The officer's name was withheld.

World.title: Winter illnesses harming students' education, NZPF president says
World.content:
Winter illnesses are harming students' education, the president of the New Zealand Principals' Federation says.

Data from the Ministry of Education showed almost 10 percent of class time was lost across the country last week due to illness. The past couple of weeks have been the worst in three years for school absences due to illness and medical reasons.

Hawke's Bay has been hit hard - one day last week, Napier Girl's High had 20 percent of its students, or about 200 girls, off due to sickness. The Terrace School - a primary in Waikpukurau - had 76 kids off on Tuesday, about a third of its roll, as well as six teachers.

NZPF president Jason Miles said absences that high affected student learning.

"You've got to work out what the children have missed in that time that they've been away. It's about the teachers knowing their children, knowing what they have missed and looking at what they can do to catch up," he told RNZ.

Have you been affected by school sickness? Get in touch at iwitness@rnz.co.nz

The principal's federation encouraged children to stay away if they were unwell, but to come back as soon as they were feeling better, he said.

"There are different communities that are hit harder than others for a period of time, and it takes 5-10 days to get over this flu, so in that time you've got a number of children who are sick, a number of children who about to get sick and of course you've got staff who are sick as well."

Illness among staff was particularly problematic, and was putting huge pressure on the relieving teacher pool, particularly in high schools.

"When you've got a lot of children away, it's fairly straightforward, but if you've got more staff away, percentage-wise, than children, then that's a really difficult space for leaders to be in, because that's about getting enough adults to keep your school open.

"So school leaders are either having to double up classes, put management staff in classes, which impacts on other parts of running the school, or rostering some years home."

Auckland Primary Principals' Association executive Lucy Naylor told the NZ Herald that parents could not afford to have a "she'll be right attitude" towards illness.

She acknowledged there could be "conflicting messaging" over when to keep children home, however.

Health NZ has official guidance for when children should not be at school.

It states: "If a child is too unwell to learn or they have an infectious illness that could spread easily to others, they need to be kept at home away from school so they can recover or get health advice or care."

World.title: Police officer injured after car rammed in Auckland
World.content:
Police say an officer has been injured when his patrol car was rammed twice in northern Auckland early on Wednesday morning.

Waitematā North Area response manager Senior Sergeant Carl Fowlie said a white ute was driving at 100km/h in a 50km/h zone in Manly, on the Whangaparāoa Peninsula.

"A patrol unit signalled for the vehicle to stop but the driver ignored instructions," Fowlie said.

"The driver then conducted a U-turn and rammed the patrol car before fleeing."

The police then pursued the driver towards Gulf Harbour but he turned his ute and rammed it into the police car again, this time head-on, Fowlie said.

"The officer received moderate injuries and was transported to hospital where they are currently being assessed."

The police vehicle was also extensively damaged.

Fowlie said the Eagle helicopter tracked the man as he scaled nearby fences, discarding items which turned out to be methamphetamine, scales and thousands of dollars in cash.

The man attempted to flag down passing vehicles without success but was caught a short time later.

"This was an incredibly dangerous act which could have resulted in serious harm to the officer who was doing their job.

"Police have zero tolerance for reckless behaviour on our roads or towards our staff, and we will hold these offenders to account," Fowlie said.

World.title: NZX appoints Hishaam Mirza as new chief executive
World.content:
The capital markets operator NZX has appointed financial services executive Hishaam Mirza to lead the company.

The NZX has been without a chief executive since May, when Mark Peterson stepped out of the role after many years of service.

NZX chair John McMahon said Mirza was a standout candidate, following a global search to lead the business, which had been struggling to grow the number of listed companies over the past decade.

"Hishaam is a proven strategic leader and recently finished a 14-year tenure at NZ Super, culminating in heading direct investments and managing a team of high-performing investment professionals," McMahon said.

"The Board is delighted with Hishaam's appointment, and we look forward to working with him in delivering NZX's growth strategy to elevate the performance of NZX and New Zealand's capital markets."

Mirza said he was up for the challenge.

"NZX is a highly trusted and well-run market at the heart of New Zealand's economy. The opportunity now is to build greater scale, liquidity and global relevance," Mirza said.

"As chief executive, I'm looking forward to ensuring the exchange - and the Smart and NZX Wealth Technologies businesses - remain strong partners for businesses, investors and government; helping New Zealand businesses grow, innovate and compete internationally, while supporting more New Zealanders to build long-term wealth."

Graham Law will continue to act as chief executive until 14 September, when Mirza takes over.

World.title: Trump seeks meeting with North Korea's Kim Jong Un before end of year
World.content:
US President Donald Trump is reportedly pushing for a meeting within the next few months with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

Trump has privately discussed setting up an in-person meeting with Kim during his next trip to Asia, The Wall Street Journal reported.

The development comes after Trump moved to "substantially reduce" US participation in joint military drills with South Korea, citing his "very good relationship" with the North Korean leader.

The drills are expected to be cut by about half, South Korean media reported.

The Ulchi Freedom Shield (UFS) exercise, which began on Sunday, had been due to run into next week.

The allies were set to complete the first, defensive phase of the exercise this week and cancel or defer a second phase involving counterattack operations, reports by broadcasters KBS, MBC, as well as newspapers Kyunghyang and DongA, said.

Trump met with Kim during his first term. AFP

Some planned field training was also expected to be postponed or cancelled, the reports said.

US Forces Korea declined to comment and referred questions to the Pentagon. The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment, while South Korea's Defence Ministry also had no immediate comment.

North Korea again denounced the drills on Wednesday, saying it would continue exercising its right to self-defence against what it called military threats from Washington and Seoul, state media KCNA reported.

A KCNA commentary called the United States and South Korea "warmongers" raising tensions on the Korean Peninsula.

It did not mention Trump, his order or the reported plans to reduce the exercise.

World.title: Hatching and scratching: What you need to know about scabies but were afraid to ask
World.content: Scabies are maddeningly itchy and - as anyone who has had them will tell you in acute detail - make you want to scrub at your skin with a wire brush. Greek philosopher Aristotle called them 'the lice of the flesh', which gives you a fair idea of what it's like to play host to these hungry critters. Scabies like to hang out all over the body, but they're most commonly found in skin folds (between fingers and toes, or in the armpits, elbow, belly button, groin area or around the waist). Having a scabies infestation often looks like a series of thin, wavy tunnels under the skin. And of course, the itch is a clear giveaway.

World.title: FIFA accused of 'management by fear' after key executive's sudden exit
World.content:
The head of Norwegian football has accused FIFA of fear tactics for the removal of a senior official who publicly opposed FIFA president Gianni Infantino's now-withdrawn World Cup sell-off plan.

Lise Klaveness, the head of the Norwegian Football Federation since 2022, told the Associated Press that the firing of FIFA's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour was "unacceptable" and urged other senior leaders to resist potentially damaging orders.

Mr Lamour's exit on Tuesday (AEST) came 17 days after his statement to AP criticising Mr Infantino's $US20 billion ($28.1 billion) private equity project, which was withdrawn hours later.

FIFA executive who criticised Infantino's World Cup sale plan departs FIFA's chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, leaves soccer's governing body, weeks after publicly criticising president Gianni Infantino.

"Now he is thrown out and we are supposed to move on. It's unacceptable, it's management by fear," Ms Klaveness told the AP in a telephone interview, describing Mr Lamour as "the best football administrator I have ever met".

"Now we also have to call upon FIFA leadership and the administration to not submit to orders you know are not in the interests of football," Ms Klaveness added, especially targeting FIFA secretary general Mattias Grafström.

Ms Klaveness represented Norway 73 times as a player, is a judge in Oslo and an elected executive committee member at European football body UEFA.

She has built on her country's long-held reputation as a champion of good governance in soccer.

Last week the Norwegian federation's board called on Mr Infantino to resign and has backed a London-based NGO's formal complaint to FIFA ethics investigators about his political ties to US President Donald Trump.

Mr Lamour was a long-time colleague of Mr Infantino, first when they were senior officials at UEFA from 2007-15. He was involved in Mr Infantino's campaign to be elected FIFA president in 2016 and moved two years ago from UEFA to oversee much of FIFA's operations in Zurich.

Infantino in crisis

Kevin Lamour (centre) said FIFA staff were "deceived" by the World Cup sell-off plan. (Getty Images: Richard Sellers)

With a reputation among the most trusted executives in the often murky world of global football politics, Mr Lamour's pointed criticisms of Mr Infantino's leadership intensified a crisis for the FIFA president.

A backlash from UEFA, the Asian Football Confederation and north American soccer body CONCACAF was provoked by a secretive plan to sell future World Cup profits to investors led by Joshua Kushner.

A $4.2 billion investment to take a 20 per cent stake in a FIFA commercial spin-off was to fund offers of $20 million to each of its 211 national member federations.

They already effectively own the non-profit soccer body, which has multi-billion dollar reserves, and would have had a mid-September deadline to accept.

Mr Lamour's statement on July 31 spoke of FIFA staff being "deceived" by Mr Infantino's lack of openness over the now-failed sale and how they "deserve better than contempt and intimidation".

The French executive called on soccer leaders worldwide "to make the right decisions".

"If that means I lose my job, then so be it," he said at the conclusion of the statement.

"I will understand and respect that decision. At least I'll sleep well tonight."

'A firing situation'

Lise Klaveness with Gianni Infantino at last month's FIFA World Cup. (Getty Images: Eva Marie Uzcategui)

Ms Klaveness said Mr Lamour's exit was "a firing situation, it's not a resignation", and suggested it was done as a result of Mr Grafström "obviously being pressured by the president".

FIFA didn't respond to a request for comment on Ms Klaveness's remarks.

In a statement, FIFA said it "thanks Kevin for his two years of service and wishes him the best of luck for the future. No further comment will be made on the matter".

Mr Lamour did not immediately reply to an email seeking comment on Wednesday (AEST).

"His statement was necessary to kill the project," Ms Klaveness said of Mr Lamour's intervention.

" He said something that was obvious, that was very important that someone within the staff told us the story so that we knew it was not FIFA, as such, but one person. "

Mr Infantino held a meeting with senior management — minus Mr Lamour — in Rabat, Morocco on August 5.

Following that, FIFA issued a statement apologising for errors and said those managers who attended "reaffirmed their full support" for Mr Infantino's presidency.

"We all got reports in Morocco, we know it's a management of fear," Ms Klaveness said.

"It's not in football's best interests."

Until the uproar over Mr Infantino's "FIFA Forward Enterprise" proposal, he seemed sure to be re-elected unopposed next year in Morocco for a fourth and final term in office through 2031.

Challengers have until November 18 to enter the contest.

Norway not discussing other candidates

Though UEFA and other critics of Mr Infantino want him ousted from the $6 million-per-year FIFA job, Ms Klaveness said any search for an opponent was not a talking point in Norway.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"We are not there at all and that is 100 per cent the truth," she said, adding that any candidate would have to be "very accountable to a governance structure that will not in four or five years just deteriorate".

Mr Infantino was appointed by UEFA in 2015 to a panel advising FIFA on reforms, in fallout from corruption scandals provoked by US federal investigations.

That group's recommendations limiting FIFA presidents to 12 years in office, plus limiting their executive powers and patronage all have retreated under Mr Infantino.

Ms Klaveness acknowledged FIFA members had been less "passionate about the details of governance" than Norway.

Mr Lamour also won praise and support from UEFA vice-president Laura McAllister, also a former player and now a university professor of governance in Wales, who lamented the "shabby events of the past weeks".

"Kevin's sacking seriously weakens FIFA's administration whilst undermining this unique opportunity to shift the culture at FIFA and to reset the organisation on sporting values, not simply commercial and financial ones," Ms McAllister said.

AP

World.title: Dees star's ban upheld as AFL tribunal rejects biomechanist evidence bid
World.content:
Melbourne has suffered a major pre-finals blow, potentially losing key forward Jacob van Rooyen for the rest of the AFL season through suspension.

The Demons failed in their bid to have van Rooyen's three-game ban for striking overturned or reduced.

It means he will miss the fifth-placed Demons' final home-and-away game on Saturday against the Western Bulldogs, and that Melbourne will need to win two finals for him to play again this season.

Van Rooyen is having a career-best season, kicking 42 goals in 22 games.

The Demons forward was charged with striking after he concussed Port Adelaide defender Aliir Aliir in a marking contest on Saturday night at the Adelaide Oval. It was graded as severe impact, careless conduct and high impact.

After the 90-minute hearing, where van Rooyen testified that he was trying to mark the ball when he collected Aliir, the tribunal jury deliberated for nearly an hour before upholding the charge.

Melbourne had argued van Rooyen's attempt to mark the ball was not careless, but the tribunal rejected their case.

Tribunal chair Jeff Gleeson KC also turned down a bid from the Demons to have a biomechanist give evidence for van Rooyen.

Aliir Aliir was left concussed after being struck in the head by van Rooyen's swinging arm. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Sarah Reed)

"The swing of van Rooyen's left arm constituted the act of a strike. It was a forceful blow. It was not simply a trailing or leading arm that Aliir collided with," Gleeson said in the verdict, adding the panel found it was careless.

"Van Rooyen was initially intending to mark the ball, but we find that shortly before impact, he ceased to intend to mark the ball. We say this despite van Rooyen's evidence to the contrary.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"Even if it was van Rooyen's sole objective at all times to contest the mark, we find that he did so in a way that failed to take reasonable care to avoid acts which could be reasonably foreseen to result in a reportable offence.

"Van Rooyen had time to move his right arm in response to seeing Aliir and he could have done so to some extent or sufficient extent with his left arm."

The tribunal also found the impact was severe and said there was potential for further injury, such as a facial fracture.

Also on Tuesday night, Brisbane AFLW key forward Dakota Davidson failed to have her one-game striking ban downgraded.

The Lions pleaded guilty and tried to argue the clash with Essendon's Maddi Gay was low rather than medium impact, but the AFLW tribunal upheld the grading.

It means one of the league's top forwards will miss the grand final rematch against two-time defending premiers North Melbourne.

AAP

World.title: Venus Williams receives US Open wildcard at 46, Serena may follow
World.content:
Venus Williams has received a US Open singles wild card and the tournament is keeping one on hold, perhaps in case her sister Serena wants to join her.

Sloane Stephens, the 2017 US Open champion, was one of six other women to receive a wild card, and the US Tennis Association said the final one was still to be announced.

That will almost certainly go to Serena Williams if she decides she wants to return to the tournament at 44.

Venus Williams received a wild card last year, returning to the grand slam event she won twice for the first time since 2023. The 46-year-old has become the oldest entrant in singles at the tournament since Renee Richards played at 47 in 1981, according to the International Tennis Federation.

Serena Williams could make her return to Flushing Meadows via the final wildcard spot. (Getty Images: Shaun Brooks/CameraSport)

She has continued to play some singles matches, and this week joined Serena for their first doubles tournament together since the 2022 US Open. They lost at the Cincinnati Open in a match tiebreaker against Marta Kostyuk and Peyton Stearns.

The sisters planned to play at Wimbledon but had to withdraw after Serena injured her knee in her singles match. That marked her first time playing singles since the 2022 US Open, and she indicated afterwards that she hoped to keep competing if she was healthy.

Headlining the wild-card recipients on the men's side are 39-year-old Gael Monfils, a past US Open semifinalist who is set to play his final grand slam tournament before retiring, and Australian Alexei Popyrin, who upset Novak Djokovic in 2024 on the way to the fourth round.

One spot is also being held among the eight men's wild cards. Stan Wawrinka, the 2016 champion at Flushing Meadows, who at 41 is playing his final season, could be a candidate for that.

Australia's Alexei Popyrin has received one of the wildcards in the men's draw. (Getty Images: Icon Sportswire/David Kirouac)

Also receiving women's wild cards were Carol Young Suh Lee, Reese Brantmeier, Thea Frodin, Leolia Jeanjean and Taylah Preston.

The other men receiving wild cards were two-time reigning NCAA singles champion Michael Zheng, Martin Damm, JJ Wolf, Sebastian Gorzny and Jack Kennedy.

Kei Nishikori, the 2014 US Open runner-up who also is retiring, was given a wild card into the men's qualifying tournament, along with Jordan Lee, Trevor Svajda, Andre Ilagan, Spencer Johnson, Michael Antonius, Andrew Johnson and Daniel Milavsky.

Women given spots in the qualifying tournament were Caroline Dolehide, Janae Preston, Katrina Scott, Ayana Akli, Annika Penickova, Julieta Pareja, Kristina Penickova and Savannah Broadus.
